questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Articulatory phonetics is INACCURATE?
options: Articulatory phonetics measures only dictionary word frequency.
The study of how speech organs produce speech sounds.
Articulators include the tongue and lips; the larynx and airflow also matter for production.
An illustration is: An investigator tracks lip closure while a person says [p].
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Articulatory phonetics measures only dictionary word frequency.”
The study of how speech organs produce speech sounds.
Example: An investigator tracks lip closure while a person says [p].
Important distinction: Articulators include the tongue and lips; the larynx and airflow also matter for production.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Acoustic phonetics is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: An investigator measures frequency and duration from a recorded vowel.
Frequency, amplitude, duration and spectral structure are acoustic properties.
The study of measurable physical properties of speech signals.
Acoustic phonetics classifies sounds solely by their written letters.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Acoustic phonetics classifies sounds solely by their written letters.”
The study of measurable physical properties of speech signals.
Example: An investigator measures frequency and duration from a recorded vowel.
Important distinction: Frequency, amplitude, duration and spectral structure are acoustic properties.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Auditory phonetics is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Listeners judge whether two recorded consonants sound different.
The auditory system receives acoustic signals, while perception also involves interpretation.
Auditory phonetics concerns only the motion of the tongue.
The study of hearing and perception of speech sounds.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Auditory phonetics concerns only the motion of the tongue.”
The study of hearing and perception of speech sounds.
Example: Listeners judge whether two recorded consonants sound different.
Important distinction: The auditory system receives acoustic signals, while perception also involves interpretation.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Pulmonic egressive airflow is INACCURATE?
options: Most English speech sounds use this mechanism, although other languages also use nonpulmonic consonants.
Ordinary English speech is primarily produced by air flowing into the lungs.
An illustration is: A person produces an ordinary English [s] while exhaling.
Speech airflow powered by air moving out from the lungs.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Ordinary English speech is primarily produced by air flowing into the lungs.”
Speech airflow powered by air moving out from the lungs.
Example: A person produces an ordinary English [s] while exhaling.
Important distinction: Most English speech sounds use this mechanism, although other languages also use nonpulmonic consonants.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Voicing is INACCURATE?
options: Voicing is defined as making a sound louder than a whisper.
Compare [z] and [s]: the key contrast is laryngeal vibration rather than loudness.
An illustration is: The folds vibrate during a sustained [z].
Vocal-fold vibration during the production of a sound.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Voicing is defined as making a sound louder than a whisper.”
Vocal-fold vibration during the production of a sound.
Example: The folds vibrate during a sustained [z].
Important distinction: Compare [z] and [s]: the key contrast is laryngeal vibration rather than loudness.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Bilabial place is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Both lips come together to produce [p], [b] or [m].
Place identifies the articulators; manner distinguishes a stop such as [p] from a nasal such as [m].
Bilabial articulation requires the tongue tip against the upper teeth.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Bilabial articulation requires the tongue tip against the upper teeth.”
Articulation involving both lips.
Example: Both lips come together to produce [p], [b] or [m].
Important distinction: Place identifies the articulators; manner distinguishes a stop such as [p] from a nasal such as [m].
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Labiodental place is INACCURATE?
options: English [f] and [v] share place and manner but differ in voicing.
An illustration is: The lower lip approaches the upper teeth for [f].
[f] is formed by complete closure of both lips.
Articulation involving the lower lip and upper teeth.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “[f] is formed by complete closure of both lips.”
Articulation involving the lower lip and upper teeth.
Example: The lower lip approaches the upper teeth for [f].
Important distinction: English [f] and [v] share place and manner but differ in voicing.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Dental place is INACCURATE?
options: Articulation involving the tongue and the teeth.
An illustration is: English [θ] in thin is produced at the teeth.
Some descriptions call these English sounds interdental; [ð] is the voiced counterpart.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “English [θ] is a bilabial nasal.”
Articulation involving the tongue and the teeth.
Example: English [θ] in thin is produced at the teeth.
Important distinction: Some descriptions call these English sounds interdental; [ð] is the voiced counterpart.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Alveolar place is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: The tongue contacts the alveolar ridge during [t].
English [t], [d], [n], [s], [z] and [l] are commonly classified as alveolar.
Alveolar sounds require closure of the vocal folds as their oral place.
Articulation at or near the ridge behind the upper teeth.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Alveolar sounds require closure of the vocal folds as their oral place.”
Articulation at or near the ridge behind the upper teeth.
Example: The tongue contacts the alveolar ridge during [t].
Important distinction: English [t], [d], [n], [s], [z] and [l] are commonly classified as alveolar.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Velar place is INACCURATE?
options: Articulation involving the tongue dorsum and soft palate.
[k], [ɡ] and [ŋ] share a velar place, though they differ in other properties.
Velar articulation is made with the upper teeth and lower lip.
An illustration is: The back of the tongue makes closure for [k].
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Velar articulation is made with the upper teeth and lower lip.”
Articulation involving the tongue dorsum and soft palate.
Example: The back of the tongue makes closure for [k].
Important distinction: [k], [ɡ] and [ŋ] share a velar place, though they differ in other properties.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Glottal place is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: The vocal folds close to produce a glottal stop [ʔ].
A glottal stop requires the lips to seal the mouth.
Glottal describes place in the larynx; it is not a synonym for a velar constriction.
Articulation whose relevant constriction is at the glottis.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A glottal stop requires the lips to seal the mouth.”
Articulation whose relevant constriction is at the glottis.
Example: The vocal folds close to produce a glottal stop [ʔ].
Important distinction: Glottal describes place in the larynx; it is not a synonym for a velar constriction.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Stop manner is INACCURATE?
options: Stops require continuous narrow-channel friction throughout their articulation.
A manner involving complete closure followed by release or another transition.
Oral stops contrast with fricatives; not every stop has a strong audible release in every context.
An illustration is: Air is briefly blocked in the mouth during [p].
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Stops require continuous narrow-channel friction throughout their articulation.”
A manner involving complete closure followed by release or another transition.
Example: Air is briefly blocked in the mouth during [p].
Important distinction: Oral stops contrast with fricatives; not every stop has a strong audible release in every context.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Fricative manner is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: A sustained [s] produces audible friction.
A manner involving turbulent airflow through a narrow constriction.
Fricatives can differ in place and voicing, as in [f], [s] and [z].
A fricative always involves an oral closure that blocks airflow completely.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A fricative always involves an oral closure that blocks airflow completely.”
A manner involving turbulent airflow through a narrow constriction.
Example: A sustained [s] produces audible friction.
Important distinction: Fricatives can differ in place and voicing, as in [f], [s] and [z].
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Affricate manner is INACCURATE?
options: A stop closure followed by a closely coordinated fricative release.
Affricates often function as single consonant units despite their complex articulation.
Every affricate is simply a vowel followed by a nasal.
An illustration is: English [tʃ] in church begins with closure and releases into friction.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every affricate is simply a vowel followed by a nasal.”
A stop closure followed by a closely coordinated fricative release.
Example: English [tʃ] in church begins with closure and releases into friction.
Important distinction: Affricates often function as single consonant units despite their complex articulation.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Nasal manner is INACCURATE?
options: Nasal consonants require the nasal passage to be completely sealed.
An illustration is: The velum is lowered during [m].
A nasal consonant typically has oral closure alongside nasal airflow.
Production with an open nasal passage so air escapes through the nose.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Nasal consonants require the nasal passage to be completely sealed.”
Production with an open nasal passage so air escapes through the nose.
Example: The velum is lowered during [m].
Important distinction: A nasal consonant typically has oral closure alongside nasal airflow.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Approximant manner is INACCURATE?
options: Glides and liquids are often grouped as approximants, with finer distinctions in their airflow.
Every approximant has the same complete closure as [p].
An illustration is: The tongue approaches the palate for [j] in yes.
Articulation with a constriction that normally does not produce fricative turbulence.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every approximant has the same complete closure as [p].”
Articulation with a constriction that normally does not produce fricative turbulence.
Example: The tongue approaches the palate for [j] in yes.
Important distinction: Glides and liquids are often grouped as approximants, with finer distinctions in their airflow.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Vowel height is INACCURATE?
options: The dimension associated with the tongue body's relative high or low position in vowel production.
An illustration is: [i] has a higher tongue position than [a].
High/close and low/open are alternative descriptive labels in vowel classification.
Vowel height is the same as a speaker's habitual loudness.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Vowel height is the same as a speaker's habitual loudness.”
The dimension associated with the tongue body's relative high or low position in vowel production.
Example: [i] has a higher tongue position than [a].
Important distinction: High/close and low/open are alternative descriptive labels in vowel classification.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Vowel backness is INACCURATE?
options: Backness means how far a written vowel appears from the end of a word.
An illustration is: [i] is front while [u] is back.
Height, backness and lip rounding jointly help describe vowel quality.
The dimension associated with the tongue body's relative front or back position.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Backness means how far a written vowel appears from the end of a word.”
The dimension associated with the tongue body's relative front or back position.
Example: [i] is front while [u] is back.
Important distinction: Height, backness and lip rounding jointly help describe vowel quality.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Lip rounding is INACCURATE?
options: Rounding is distinct from backness: front rounded vowels occur in many languages.
An illustration is: A typical [u] is produced with rounded lips.
The protrusion or rounding of the lips during speech.
All vowels in all languages must be rounded.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “All vowels in all languages must be rounded.”
The protrusion or rounding of the lips during speech.
Example: A typical [u] is produced with rounded lips.
Important distinction: Rounding is distinct from backness: front rounded vowels occur in many languages.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Diphthong is INACCURATE?
options: A diphthong must consist of two separate syllables.
An illustration is: The vowel of many English pronunciations of my glides as [aɪ].
A vowel with a noticeable quality change within one syllable.
Accent matters: vowel realizations and phonemic analyses differ across English varieties.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A diphthong must consist of two separate syllables.”
A vowel with a noticeable quality change within one syllable.
Example: The vowel of many English pronunciations of my glides as [aɪ].
Important distinction: Accent matters: vowel realizations and phonemic analyses differ across English varieties.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Schwa is INACCURATE?
options: Schwa is the IPA symbol for a voiceless bilabial stop.
Schwa's distribution varies by language and accent; it is not inherently unstressed in every language.
The mid central vowel represented by [ə], often occurring in unstressed syllables in English.
An illustration is: Many English speakers use [ə] in the first syllable of about.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Schwa is the IPA symbol for a voiceless bilabial stop.”
The mid central vowel represented by [ə], often occurring in unstressed syllables in English.
Example: Many English speakers use [ə] in the first syllable of about.
Important distinction: Schwa's distribution varies by language and accent; it is not inherently unstressed in every language.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Phone is INACCURATE?
options: Square brackets conventionally mark phonetic transcription.
An illustration is: An analyst transcribes an actual aspirated release as [pʰ].
A speech sound considered as a physical phonetic realization.
A phone is a written letter of an alphabet.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A phone is a written letter of an alphabet.”
A speech sound considered as a physical phonetic realization.
Example: An analyst transcribes an actual aspirated release as [pʰ].
Important distinction: Square brackets conventionally mark phonetic transcription.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Phoneme is INACCURATE?
options: Contrast is language-specific; a phoneme is an abstract category rather than a single identical waveform.
A contrastive unit in a language's sound system.
Two sounds belong to different phonemes whenever their waveforms differ at all.
An illustration is: Substituting /b/ for /p/ changes pat to bat in English.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Two sounds belong to different phonemes whenever their waveforms differ at all.”
A contrastive unit in a language's sound system.
Example: Substituting /b/ for /p/ changes pat to bat in English.
Important distinction: Contrast is language-specific; a phoneme is an abstract category rather than a single identical waveform.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Allophone is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: English /p/ is aspirated in pin but typically unaspirated after /s/ in spin.
The same phonetic distinction can be allophonic in one language and phonemic in another.
A contextually or otherwise conditioned realization of a phoneme that does not by itself create a lexical contrast in that system.
English [pʰ] and [p] must distinguish words in every position.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “English [pʰ] and [p] must distinguish words in every position.”
A contextually or otherwise conditioned realization of a phoneme that does not by itself create a lexical contrast in that system.
Example: English /p/ is aspirated in pin but typically unaspirated after /s/ in spin.
Important distinction: The same phonetic distinction can be allophonic in one language and phonemic in another.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Minimal pair is INACCURATE?
options: Two words differing in one sound in the same position with a difference in meaning.
Minimal pairs provide strong evidence for phonemic contrast in the language being analyzed.
An illustration is: English sip and zip differ only in their initial consonants.
Two words form a minimal pair whenever they rhyme, regardless of other differences.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Two words form a minimal pair whenever they rhyme, regardless of other differences.”
Two words differing in one sound in the same position with a difference in meaning.
Example: English sip and zip differ only in their initial consonants.
Important distinction: Minimal pairs provide strong evidence for phonemic contrast in the language being analyzed.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Complementary distribution is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Aspirated and unaspirated English voiceless stops follow predictable environments in a simplified analysis.
Distribution supports an allophonic analysis when phonetic similarity and other evidence also fit.
A pattern in which two sounds occur in mutually exclusive environments.
Complementary distribution means the sounds occur in exactly the same environments.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Complementary distribution means the sounds occur in exactly the same environments.”
A pattern in which two sounds occur in mutually exclusive environments.
Example: Aspirated and unaspirated English voiceless stops follow predictable environments in a simplified analysis.
Important distinction: Distribution supports an allophonic analysis when phonetic similarity and other evidence also fit.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Broad transcription is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: An English word is written with /p/ without marking aspiration.
A transcription emphasizing contrastive categories while omitting much phonetic detail.
Broad transcription must record every small articulatory detail.
Slashes commonly mark phonemic transcription; narrow phonetic detail is usually bracketed.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Broad transcription must record every small articulatory detail.”
A transcription emphasizing contrastive categories while omitting much phonetic detail.
Example: An English word is written with /p/ without marking aspiration.
Important distinction: Slashes commonly mark phonemic transcription; narrow phonetic detail is usually bracketed.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Narrow transcription is INACCURATE?
options: Narrow transcription is defined by the use of ordinary spelling alone.
A transcription including comparatively detailed phonetic properties.
Diacritics can mark aspiration, nasalization and other details relevant to an analysis.
An illustration is: An analyst writes [pʰ] to mark aspiration explicitly.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Narrow transcription is defined by the use of ordinary spelling alone.”
A transcription including comparatively detailed phonetic properties.
Example: An analyst writes [pʰ] to mark aspiration explicitly.
Important distinction: Diacritics can mark aspiration, nasalization and other details relevant to an analysis.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Spectrogram is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Time runs horizontally and frequency vertically, with shading representing energy.
The vertical axis of a conventional spectrogram represents grammatical tense.
Display settings affect appearance, so darkness is not a universal ranking of all vowels above all consonants.
A display showing how a signal's spectral energy varies over time.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “The vertical axis of a conventional spectrogram represents grammatical tense.”
A display showing how a signal's spectral energy varies over time.
Example: Time runs horizontally and frequency vertically, with shading representing energy.
Important distinction: Display settings affect appearance, so darkness is not a universal ranking of all vowels above all consonants.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Formants is INACCURATE?
options: Formants are identical to the repetition rate of vocal-fold vibration.
An illustration is: An analyst compares F1 and F2 to investigate vowel quality.
Fundamental frequency concerns periodicity; formants concern resonances shaped by the vocal tract.
Resonant frequency regions of the vocal tract reflected in the speech spectrum.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Formants are identical to the repetition rate of vocal-fold vibration.”
Resonant frequency regions of the vocal tract reflected in the speech spectrum.
Example: An analyst compares F1 and F2 to investigate vowel quality.
Important distinction: Fundamental frequency concerns periodicity; formants concern resonances shaped by the vocal tract.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Fundamental frequency is INACCURATE?
options: The repetition rate of a periodic waveform, related in voiced speech to vocal-fold vibration.
Fundamental frequency is measured in seconds and means segment duration.
Perceived pitch is related to fundamental frequency, but physical and perceptual measures are not identical.
An illustration is: A voiced segment has a fundamental frequency measured in hertz.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Fundamental frequency is measured in seconds and means segment duration.”
The repetition rate of a periodic waveform, related in voiced speech to vocal-fold vibration.
Example: A voiced segment has a fundamental frequency measured in hertz.
Important distinction: Perceived pitch is related to fundamental frequency, but physical and perceptual measures are not identical.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Stress is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: The first syllable is prominent in the English noun REcord.
Relative prominence assigned to syllables within words or larger structures.
Duration, pitch and intensity can contribute to stress, with language-specific patterns.
Stress is determined entirely by which letters are capitalized in normal spelling.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Stress is determined entirely by which letters are capitalized in normal spelling.”
Relative prominence assigned to syllables within words or larger structures.
Example: The first syllable is prominent in the English noun REcord.
Important distinction: Duration, pitch and intensity can contribute to stress, with language-specific patterns.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Intonation is INACCURATE?
options: Contour interpretation depends on construction, language, variety and context.
An illustration is: A speaker changes a sentence's pitch contour to convey a particular interactional stance.
Patterns of pitch variation over phrases or utterances.
Every question in every language must have rising intonation.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every question in every language must have rising intonation.”
Patterns of pitch variation over phrases or utterances.
Example: A speaker changes a sentence's pitch contour to convey a particular interactional stance.
Important distinction: Contour interpretation depends on construction, language, variety and context.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Assimilation is INACCURATE?
options: Coarticulatory pressures often motivate assimilation, but the precise patterns are language-specific.
Assimilation means a sound must become less like its neighbour.
A process in which one sound becomes more similar to a nearby sound.
An illustration is: In casual speech, an alveolar nasal may become bilabial before a bilabial consonant.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Assimilation means a sound must become less like its neighbour.”
A process in which one sound becomes more similar to a nearby sound.
Example: In casual speech, an alveolar nasal may become bilabial before a bilabial consonant.
Important distinction: Coarticulatory pressures often motivate assimilation, but the precise patterns are language-specific.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Phonotactics is INACCURATE?
options: A cluster impossible in English must be impossible in every language.
Constraints on permissible sound sequences and syllable patterns in a language.
An illustration is: English allows /str/ at the start of street but not every imaginable initial cluster.
Phonotactic restrictions differ across languages and concern patterns beyond individual sound inventories.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A cluster impossible in English must be impossible in every language.”
Constraints on permissible sound sequences and syllable patterns in a language.
Example: English allows /str/ at the start of street but not every imaginable initial cluster.
Important distinction: Phonotactic restrictions differ across languages and concern patterns beyond individual sound inventories.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Postalveolar place is INACCURATE?
options: Some introductory books use broader palatal labels; more precise IPA descriptions separate postalveolar and palatal places.
Articulation just behind the alveolar ridge.
English [ʃ] must be produced with both lips fully closed.
An illustration is: English [ʃ] in ship is commonly described as postalveolar.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “English [ʃ] must be produced with both lips fully closed.”
Articulation just behind the alveolar ridge.
Example: English [ʃ] in ship is commonly described as postalveolar.
Important distinction: Some introductory books use broader palatal labels; more precise IPA descriptions separate postalveolar and palatal places.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Palatal place is INACCURATE?
options: Articulation involving the tongue body and the hard palate.
A palatal consonant is defined by contact between the lower lip and upper teeth.
An illustration is: [j] in yes is a palatal approximant.
Palatal [j] differs in place from the velar consonant [k].
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A palatal consonant is defined by contact between the lower lip and upper teeth.”
Articulation involving the tongue body and the hard palate.
Example: [j] in yes is a palatal approximant.
Important distinction: Palatal [j] differs in place from the velar consonant [k].
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Lateral approximant is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: English [l] allows lateral oral airflow.
An approximant whose airflow passes around one or both sides of the tongue.
A lateral approximant requires all airflow to pass only through the nose.
Lateral refers to airflow; English /l/ can have different context-dependent realizations.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A lateral approximant requires all airflow to pass only through the nose.”
An approximant whose airflow passes around one or both sides of the tongue.
Example: English [l] allows lateral oral airflow.
Important distinction: Lateral refers to airflow; English /l/ can have different context-dependent realizations.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Aspiration is INACCURATE?
options: Aspiration is identical to the voiced vibration of [z].
A period of voiceless airflow associated with the release of a stop, marked [ʰ] in IPA.
An illustration is: The [pʰ] in a typical stressed English pin has an audible puff of air.
In English it is often predictable for voiceless stops; its contrastive status differs across languages.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Aspiration is identical to the voiced vibration of [z].”
A period of voiceless airflow associated with the release of a stop, marked [ʰ] in IPA.
Example: The [pʰ] in a typical stressed English pin has an audible puff of air.
Important distinction: In English it is often predictable for voiceless stops; its contrastive status differs across languages.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Syllable structure is INACCURATE?
options: The nucleus is the sonority peak; some languages permit syllabic consonants.
An illustration is: Cat has /k/ as onset, /æ/ as nucleus and /t/ as coda in a simple analysis.
Every syllable in every language must contain an overt consonant onset.
Organization of segments into units commonly analyzed as onset, nucleus and coda.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every syllable in every language must contain an overt consonant onset.”
Organization of segments into units commonly analyzed as onset, nucleus and coda.
Example: Cat has /k/ as onset, /æ/ as nucleus and /t/ as coda in a simple analysis.
Important distinction: The nucleus is the sonority peak; some languages permit syllabic consonants.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Amplitude and intensity is INACCURATE?
options: Loudness is a perceptual correlate, not simply another name for a physical amplitude measurement.
Greater amplitude by definition means that a word has more morphemes.
An illustration is: A sound recording displays greater waveform excursions when amplitude increases.
Related physical measures associated with signal magnitude and energy.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Greater amplitude by definition means that a word has more morphemes.”
Related physical measures associated with signal magnitude and energy.
Example: A sound recording displays greater waveform excursions when amplitude increases.
Important distinction: Loudness is a perceptual correlate, not simply another name for a physical amplitude measurement.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which statement about Duration is INACCURATE?
options: The time interval occupied by an event or speech segment.
Duration is measured in hertz rather than units of time.
An illustration is: A vowel lasts 150 milliseconds in a recorded token.
Physical duration can affect contrasts, stress and rhythm, depending on the language.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Duration is measured in hertz rather than units of time.”
The time interval occupied by an event or speech segment.
Example: A vowel lasts 150 milliseconds in a recorded token.
Important distinction: Physical duration can affect contrasts, stress and rhythm, depending on the language.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Pin and spin show aspirated versus unaspirated realizations of English /p/. What does this primarily illustrate?
options: A minimal pair differing only in aspiration.
questions.explanation: The words differ in more than aspiration, so they are not a minimal pair testing aspiration. English aspiration here follows the phonological environment.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which property primarily distinguishes a formant from fundamental frequency?
options: A formant reflects vocal-tract resonance, while F0 reflects periodicity.
Both are names for the number of letters.
A formant is spelling, while F0 is grammar.
F0 can only be measured in milliseconds.
questions.explanation: The source-filter distinction separates laryngeal periodicity from resonances of the vocal tract. F1 and F2 are especially useful for analyzing vowel quality.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question: Which inference is valid when English disallows a particular initial cluster?
options: Every speaker is physically unable to articulate it.
The written alphabet determines all permitted clusters.
The restriction is a fact about English phonotactics, not proof of a universal impossibility.
The cluster cannot occur in any natural language.
questions.explanation: Languages differ in permitted sound sequences. A sequence absent from one system can be ordinary in another; physical production and linguistic licensing differ.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
The smallest unit with a meaning or grammatical function in a morphological analysis.
questions.explanation:
The smallest unit with a meaning or grammatical function in a morphological analysis.
Example: Cats contains cat and a plural marker.
Important distinction: A morpheme may be free or bound; grammatical meaning counts even without a concrete object referent.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
An observable form realizing a morpheme.
questions.explanation:
An observable form realizing a morpheme.
Example: The sound [s] realizes the plural morpheme in cats.
Important distinction: Morpheme names the analytical unit; morph identifies its realization in a particular form.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
An alternative realization of the same morpheme.
questions.explanation:
An alternative realization of the same morpheme.
Example: English regular plurals have [s], [z] and [ɪz] realizations.
Important distinction: Allomorphs preserve the relevant grammatical contribution despite differences in form.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A morpheme capable of occurring as a word on its own.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme capable of occurring as a word on its own.
Example: Book can occur alone and also inside books.
Important distinction: A complex word such as duster is not a single free morpheme merely because it can stand alone.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A morpheme that cannot ordinarily occur independently as a word.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme that cannot ordinarily occur independently as a word.
Example: The past-tense suffix -ed attaches to a verbal base.
Important distinction: Affixes are bound, but bound roots also occur, so bound morpheme and affix are not exact synonyms.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A morpheme contributing substantial content meaning.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme contributing substantial content meaning.
Example: The root tiger contributes the animal concept in tigers.
Important distinction: Lexical roots often belong to open classes such as nouns, verbs and adjectives.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A morpheme contributing grammatical organization or relational information.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme contributing grammatical organization or relational information.
Example: The article the marks a noun phrase as definite in a suitable context.
Important distinction: The category includes free function words and, in broader usage, bound grammatical markers.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
Morphology forming a new lexeme or a new lexical meaning, sometimes changing word class.
questions.explanation:
Morphology forming a new lexeme or a new lexical meaning, sometimes changing word class.
Example: Adding un- to happy creates unhappy.
Important distinction: Unhappy remains an adjective; category preservation does not prevent an operation from being derivational.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Morphology expressing grammatical contrasts within a lexeme's paradigm.
questions.explanation:
Morphology expressing grammatical contrasts within a lexeme's paradigm.
Example: Walk and walked express different grammatical forms of the same verb.
Important distinction: Inflection generally preserves lexical category and core lexical identity.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
An affix attached before its base.
questions.explanation:
An affix attached before its base.
Example: Re- precedes write in rewrite.
Important distinction: Position defines a prefix; whether it is derivational or inflectional depends on its function in the language.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
An affix attached after its base.
questions.explanation:
An affix attached after its base.
Example: -ness follows kind in kindness.
Important distinction: English suffixes can be derivational or inflectional, as -ness and plural -s illustrate.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
An affix inserted within a root or base.
questions.explanation:
An affix inserted within a root or base.
Example: Tagalog sulat and sumulat illustrate an inserted -um-.
Important distinction: Men illustrates internal vowel change; genuine infixation requires an inserted morphological element.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
The basic lexical core remaining after relevant affixes are removed.
questions.explanation:
The basic lexical core remaining after relevant affixes are removed.
Example: Help is the root in unhelpfulness.
Important distinction: Roots can be free or bound; not every root can occur as an independent word.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A form to which a morphological operation applies.
questions.explanation:
A form to which a morphological operation applies.
Example: Helpful is the base to which un- attaches in unhelpful.
Important distinction: A base may be a root or an already complex form.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A form to which an inflectional operation applies in a common introductory usage.
questions.explanation:
A form to which an inflectional operation applies in a common introductory usage.
Example: Worker is the stem receiving plural -s in workers.
Important distinction: Stem and base terminology varies somewhat across frameworks; the intended definition should be stated.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English plural ending.
questions.explanation:
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English plural ending.
Example: Dogs ends in [z], cats in [s], and buses in [ɪz] in many descriptions.
Important distinction: A sibilant requires the syllabic variant; otherwise the preceding segment's voicing normally conditions the ending.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English past-tense ending.
questions.explanation:
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English past-tense ending.
Example: Walked has [t], played [d], and wanted [ɪd] in common transcriptions.
Important distinction: The syllabic variant follows /t/ or /d/; other environments condition [t] or [d].
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A morphological relation involving forms with substantially different roots.
questions.explanation:
A morphological relation involving forms with substantially different roots.
Example: Go and went are related as present and past forms of one verb.
Important distinction: The relation is grammatical despite the absence of an ordinary predictable shared root shape.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A plural form without an overt plural affix in an appropriate analysis.
questions.explanation:
A plural form without an overt plural affix in an appropriate analysis.
Example: One sheep and three sheep share the same overt noun form.
Important distinction: Number can be identified from syntax and context even when the noun has no overt plural marker.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A morphological pattern realized by changing a vowel inside a base.
questions.explanation:
A morphological pattern realized by changing a vowel inside a base.
Example: Sing, sang and sung differ in their internal vowels.
Important distinction: Internal modification differs from concatenating a separate prefix or suffix.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Formation of a word from two or more lexical bases.
questions.explanation:
Formation of a word from two or more lexical bases.
Example: Toothbrush combines tooth and brush.
Important distinction: Spacing and hyphenation do not reliably determine compound status on their own.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A change in lexical category without an overt derivational affix.
questions.explanation:
A change in lexical category without an overt derivational affix.
Example: The noun bottle is used as a verb in They bottle the juice.
Important distinction: Also called zero derivation in some accounts, this process requires attention to actual use and analysis.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
The number of meaningful or grammatical units identified in a word.
questions.explanation:
The number of meaningful or grammatical units identified in a word.
Example: Unhelpful contains three units: un-, help and -ful.
Important distinction: Teacher has two morphemes, while some multisyllabic words such as banana are monomorphemic.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A common English ordering in which derivation is nearer the root than outer inflection.
questions.explanation:
A common English ordering in which derivation is nearer the root than outer inflection.
Example: Workers has work + -er + plural -s.
Important distinction: Morphological hierarchy matters; this English tendency should not be universalized without qualification.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A phrase headed by a noun or nominal element in a traditional introductory analysis.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by a noun or nominal element in a traditional introductory analysis.
Example: The very old house functions as subject in The very old house collapsed.
Important distinction: A single noun or pronoun can form a phrase; determiner-phrase analyses provide a different theoretical treatment.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A phrase headed by a preposition, often with a complement.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by a preposition, often with a complement.
Example: Under the table contains the preposition under and its complement.
Important distinction: Phrase category follows the head; grammatical function and phrase category must be distinguished.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A phrase headed by an adjective.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by an adjective.
Example: Very proud of her work is headed by proud.
Important distinction: Nice blue shirt is a noun phrase; adjective modifiers do not change its nominal head.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A phrase headed by an adverb.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by an adverb.
Example: Quite slowly is headed by slowly.
Important distinction: In a loud voice is a prepositional phrase that may function as an adverbial.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A phrase headed by a verb, with its dependents according to the framework used.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by a verb, with its dependents according to the framework used.
Example: Has eaten the apple includes a verbal head and its object in a common syntactic analysis.
Important distinction: Some school grammars use a narrower verb-group label; state the adopted framework when boundaries matter.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A nonfinite construction based on an infinitive verb.
questions.explanation:
A nonfinite construction based on an infinitive verb.
Example: To read novels functions as the complement of likes in She likes to read novels.
Important distinction: Many modern grammars treat such units as nonfinite clauses rather than simply infinitive phrases.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A nonfinite -ing construction traditionally associated with a nominal function.
questions.explanation:
A nonfinite -ing construction traditionally associated with a nominal function.
Example: Reading novels is relaxing places reading novels in subject position.
Important distinction: Compare a progressive verb in is reading; modern analyses often use a unified gerund-participial category.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A participial construction modifying a nominal expression or supplying supplementary information.
questions.explanation:
A participial construction modifying a nominal expression or supplying supplementary information.
Example: The child wearing a red hat waved uses wearing a red hat to modify child.
Important distinction: Restrictive modifiers often lack commas; supplementary participial constructions are commonly set off.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A supplementary construction with its own subject-like element, often without a finite verb.
questions.explanation:
A supplementary construction with its own subject-like element, often without a finite verb.
Example: Her eyes on the clock, Sara waited for the bus.
Important distinction: The construction comments on the accompanying situation; her eyes and on the clock form its internal relation.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A clause capable of functioning as a complete sentence in ordinary use.
questions.explanation:
A clause capable of functioning as a complete sentence in ordinary use.
Example: Tara ate a cheese roll can stand independently.
Important distinction: Independence concerns syntactic status, not whether a reader needs any wider context to understand a reference.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A clause syntactically subordinate to another construction.
questions.explanation:
A clause syntactically subordinate to another construction.
Example: After she watched the news is subordinate in Tara ate after she watched the news.
Important distinction: Finite subordinate clauses often have an overt subject and verb, while nonfinite clauses may omit an overt subject.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A hierarchy of grammatical units in a stated framework.
questions.explanation:
A hierarchy of grammatical units in a stated framework.
Example: Sentence, clause, phrase, word and morpheme are arranged from larger to smaller units in an introductory scale.
Important distinction: Syntax names a field or level of analysis, not a unit equivalent to sentence on this scale.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A word class that readily admits new members.
questions.explanation:
A word class that readily admits new members.
Example: English gains new nouns and verbs for new technologies.
Important distinction: Openness is a tendency; nouns, verbs and adjectives are common examples.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A word class with relatively limited membership and limited ready addition.
questions.explanation:
A word class with relatively limited membership and limited ready addition.
Example: English personal pronouns form a comparatively restricted inventory.
Important distinction: Closed means comparatively resistant to expansion, not eternally frozen.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
The conventional introductory list of eight English inflectional suffix categories.
questions.explanation:
The conventional introductory list of eight English inflectional suffix categories.
Example: Plural, possessive, third-person singular, past tense, two participles, comparative and superlative are listed.
Important distinction: Comparative -er in taller is inflectional; the similar-looking agentive -er is derivational.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Forming a word by combining portions of existing words.
questions.explanation:
Forming a word by combining portions of existing words.
Example: Brunch combines parts of breakfast and lunch.
Important distinction: It differs from ordinary compounding in which whole lexical bases are combined.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
Forming a shorter lexical form by shortening an existing word.
questions.explanation:
Forming a shorter lexical form by shortening an existing word.
Example: Exam is a shortened form of examination.
Important distinction: Shortening does not necessarily change the word's core referential meaning or category.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Forming a word from initial letters that is pronounced as a word in a narrow usage.
questions.explanation:
Forming a word from initial letters that is pronounced as a word in a narrow usage.
Example: NASA is pronounced as a word rather than as a sequence of individual letter names.
Important distinction: Terminology varies; the narrow contrast distinguishes acronyms from initialisms such as BBC.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Adoption of a linguistic form from another language.
questions.explanation:
Adoption of a linguistic form from another language.
Example: English uses bungalow, historically borrowed from an Indian-language source.
Important distinction: Borrowings often become adapted to the receiving language's sounds and morphology.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which ordering correctly represents units from larger to smaller in a common introductory rank scale?
questions.explanation: The rank scale orders grammatical units. Syntax and phonetics name fields or levels of analysis, not unit ranks parallel to word or clause.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Cats contains cat and a plural marker.
questions.explanation:
The smallest unit with a meaning or grammatical function in a morphological analysis.
Example: Cats contains cat and a plural marker.
Important distinction: A morpheme may be free or bound; grammatical meaning counts even without a concrete object referent.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
The sound [s] realizes the plural morpheme in cats.
questions.explanation:
An observable form realizing a morpheme.
Example: The sound [s] realizes the plural morpheme in cats.
Important distinction: Morpheme names the analytical unit; morph identifies its realization in a particular form.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
English regular plurals have [s], [z] and [ɪz] realizations.
questions.explanation:
An alternative realization of the same morpheme.
Example: English regular plurals have [s], [z] and [ɪz] realizations.
Important distinction: Allomorphs preserve the relevant grammatical contribution despite differences in form.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Book can occur alone and also inside books.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme capable of occurring as a word on its own.
Example: Book can occur alone and also inside books.
Important distinction: A complex word such as duster is not a single free morpheme merely because it can stand alone.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
The past-tense suffix -ed attaches to a verbal base.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme that cannot ordinarily occur independently as a word.
Example: The past-tense suffix -ed attaches to a verbal base.
Important distinction: Affixes are bound, but bound roots also occur, so bound morpheme and affix are not exact synonyms.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
The root tiger contributes the animal concept in tigers.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme contributing substantial content meaning.
Example: The root tiger contributes the animal concept in tigers.
Important distinction: Lexical roots often belong to open classes such as nouns, verbs and adjectives.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
The article the marks a noun phrase as definite in a suitable context.
questions.explanation:
A morpheme contributing grammatical organization or relational information.
Example: The article the marks a noun phrase as definite in a suitable context.
Important distinction: The category includes free function words and, in broader usage, bound grammatical markers.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Adding un- to happy creates unhappy.
questions.explanation:
Morphology forming a new lexeme or a new lexical meaning, sometimes changing word class.
Example: Adding un- to happy creates unhappy.
Important distinction: Unhappy remains an adjective; category preservation does not prevent an operation from being derivational.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Walk and walked express different grammatical forms of the same verb.
questions.explanation:
Morphology expressing grammatical contrasts within a lexeme's paradigm.
Example: Walk and walked express different grammatical forms of the same verb.
Important distinction: Inflection generally preserves lexical category and core lexical identity.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Re- precedes write in rewrite.
questions.explanation:
An affix attached before its base.
Example: Re- precedes write in rewrite.
Important distinction: Position defines a prefix; whether it is derivational or inflectional depends on its function in the language.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
-ness follows kind in kindness.
questions.explanation:
An affix attached after its base.
Example: -ness follows kind in kindness.
Important distinction: English suffixes can be derivational or inflectional, as -ness and plural -s illustrate.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Tagalog sulat and sumulat illustrate an inserted -um-.
questions.explanation:
An affix inserted within a root or base.
Example: Tagalog sulat and sumulat illustrate an inserted -um-.
Important distinction: Men illustrates internal vowel change; genuine infixation requires an inserted morphological element.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Help is the root in unhelpfulness.
questions.explanation:
The basic lexical core remaining after relevant affixes are removed.
Example: Help is the root in unhelpfulness.
Important distinction: Roots can be free or bound; not every root can occur as an independent word.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Helpful is the base to which un- attaches in unhelpful.
questions.explanation:
A form to which a morphological operation applies.
Example: Helpful is the base to which un- attaches in unhelpful.
Important distinction: A base may be a root or an already complex form.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Worker is the stem receiving plural -s in workers.
questions.explanation:
A form to which an inflectional operation applies in a common introductory usage.
Example: Worker is the stem receiving plural -s in workers.
Important distinction: Stem and base terminology varies somewhat across frameworks; the intended definition should be stated.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Dogs ends in [z], cats in [s], and buses in [ɪz] in many descriptions.
questions.explanation:
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English plural ending.
Example: Dogs ends in [z], cats in [s], and buses in [ɪz] in many descriptions.
Important distinction: A sibilant requires the syllabic variant; otherwise the preceding segment's voicing normally conditions the ending.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Walked has [t], played [d], and wanted [ɪd] in common transcriptions.
questions.explanation:
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English past-tense ending.
Example: Walked has [t], played [d], and wanted [ɪd] in common transcriptions.
Important distinction: The syllabic variant follows /t/ or /d/; other environments condition [t] or [d].
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Go and went are related as present and past forms of one verb.
questions.explanation:
A morphological relation involving forms with substantially different roots.
Example: Go and went are related as present and past forms of one verb.
Important distinction: The relation is grammatical despite the absence of an ordinary predictable shared root shape.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
One sheep and three sheep share the same overt noun form.
questions.explanation:
A plural form without an overt plural affix in an appropriate analysis.
Example: One sheep and three sheep share the same overt noun form.
Important distinction: Number can be identified from syntax and context even when the noun has no overt plural marker.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Sing, sang and sung differ in their internal vowels.
questions.explanation:
A morphological pattern realized by changing a vowel inside a base.
Example: Sing, sang and sung differ in their internal vowels.
Important distinction: Internal modification differs from concatenating a separate prefix or suffix.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Toothbrush combines tooth and brush.
questions.explanation:
Formation of a word from two or more lexical bases.
Example: Toothbrush combines tooth and brush.
Important distinction: Spacing and hyphenation do not reliably determine compound status on their own.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
The noun bottle is used as a verb in They bottle the juice.
questions.explanation:
A change in lexical category without an overt derivational affix.
Example: The noun bottle is used as a verb in They bottle the juice.
Important distinction: Also called zero derivation in some accounts, this process requires attention to actual use and analysis.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Unhelpful contains three units: un-, help and -ful.
questions.explanation:
The number of meaningful or grammatical units identified in a word.
Example: Unhelpful contains three units: un-, help and -ful.
Important distinction: Teacher has two morphemes, while some multisyllabic words such as banana are monomorphemic.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Workers has work + -er + plural -s.
questions.explanation:
A common English ordering in which derivation is nearer the root than outer inflection.
Example: Workers has work + -er + plural -s.
Important distinction: Morphological hierarchy matters; this English tendency should not be universalized without qualification.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
The very old house functions as subject in The very old house collapsed.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by a noun or nominal element in a traditional introductory analysis.
Example: The very old house functions as subject in The very old house collapsed.
Important distinction: A single noun or pronoun can form a phrase; determiner-phrase analyses provide a different theoretical treatment.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Under the table contains the preposition under and its complement.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by a preposition, often with a complement.
Example: Under the table contains the preposition under and its complement.
Important distinction: Phrase category follows the head; grammatical function and phrase category must be distinguished.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Very proud of her work is headed by proud.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by an adjective.
Example: Very proud of her work is headed by proud.
Important distinction: Nice blue shirt is a noun phrase; adjective modifiers do not change its nominal head.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Quite slowly is headed by slowly.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by an adverb.
Example: Quite slowly is headed by slowly.
Important distinction: In a loud voice is a prepositional phrase that may function as an adverbial.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Has eaten the apple includes a verbal head and its object in a common syntactic analysis.
questions.explanation:
A phrase headed by a verb, with its dependents according to the framework used.
Example: Has eaten the apple includes a verbal head and its object in a common syntactic analysis.
Important distinction: Some school grammars use a narrower verb-group label; state the adopted framework when boundaries matter.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
To read novels functions as the complement of likes in She likes to read novels.
questions.explanation:
A nonfinite construction based on an infinitive verb.
Example: To read novels functions as the complement of likes in She likes to read novels.
Important distinction: Many modern grammars treat such units as nonfinite clauses rather than simply infinitive phrases.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Reading novels is relaxing places reading novels in subject position.
questions.explanation:
A nonfinite -ing construction traditionally associated with a nominal function.
Example: Reading novels is relaxing places reading novels in subject position.
Important distinction: Compare a progressive verb in is reading; modern analyses often use a unified gerund-participial category.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
The child wearing a red hat waved uses wearing a red hat to modify child.
questions.explanation:
A participial construction modifying a nominal expression or supplying supplementary information.
Example: The child wearing a red hat waved uses wearing a red hat to modify child.
Important distinction: Restrictive modifiers often lack commas; supplementary participial constructions are commonly set off.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Her eyes on the clock, Sara waited for the bus.
questions.explanation:
A supplementary construction with its own subject-like element, often without a finite verb.
Example: Her eyes on the clock, Sara waited for the bus.
Important distinction: The construction comments on the accompanying situation; her eyes and on the clock form its internal relation.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Tara ate a cheese roll can stand independently.
questions.explanation:
A clause capable of functioning as a complete sentence in ordinary use.
Example: Tara ate a cheese roll can stand independently.
Important distinction: Independence concerns syntactic status, not whether a reader needs any wider context to understand a reference.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
After she watched the news is subordinate in Tara ate after she watched the news.
questions.explanation:
A clause syntactically subordinate to another construction.
Example: After she watched the news is subordinate in Tara ate after she watched the news.
Important distinction: Finite subordinate clauses often have an overt subject and verb, while nonfinite clauses may omit an overt subject.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Sentence, clause, phrase, word and morpheme are arranged from larger to smaller units in an introductory scale.
questions.explanation:
A hierarchy of grammatical units in a stated framework.
Example: Sentence, clause, phrase, word and morpheme are arranged from larger to smaller units in an introductory scale.
Important distinction: Syntax names a field or level of analysis, not a unit equivalent to sentence on this scale.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
English gains new nouns and verbs for new technologies.
questions.explanation:
A word class that readily admits new members.
Example: English gains new nouns and verbs for new technologies.
Important distinction: Openness is a tendency; nouns, verbs and adjectives are common examples.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
English personal pronouns form a comparatively restricted inventory.
questions.explanation:
A word class with relatively limited membership and limited ready addition.
Example: English personal pronouns form a comparatively restricted inventory.
Important distinction: Closed means comparatively resistant to expansion, not eternally frozen.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
Plural, possessive, third-person singular, past tense, two participles, comparative and superlative are listed.
questions.explanation:
The conventional introductory list of eight English inflectional suffix categories.
Example: Plural, possessive, third-person singular, past tense, two participles, comparative and superlative are listed.
Important distinction: Comparative -er in taller is inflectional; the similar-looking agentive -er is derivational.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
Brunch combines parts of breakfast and lunch.
questions.explanation:
Forming a word by combining portions of existing words.
Example: Brunch combines parts of breakfast and lunch.
Important distinction: It differs from ordinary compounding in which whole lexical bases are combined.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Read the case and choose the most appropriate concept.
Exam is a shortened form of examination.
questions.explanation:
Forming a shorter lexical form by shortening an existing word.
Example: Exam is a shortened form of examination.
Important distinction: Shortening does not necessarily change the word's core referential meaning or category.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which concept is most directly illustrated by this example?
NASA is pronounced as a word rather than as a sequence of individual letter names.
questions.explanation:
Forming a word from initial letters that is pronounced as a word in a narrow usage.
Example: NASA is pronounced as a word rather than as a sequence of individual letter names.
Important distinction: Terminology varies; the narrow contrast distinguishes acronyms from initialisms such as BBC.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Which analysis best identifies the main concept in this case?
English uses bungalow, historically borrowed from an Indian-language source.
questions.explanation:
Adoption of a linguistic form from another language.
Example: English uses bungalow, historically borrowed from an Indian-language source.
Important distinction: Borrowings often become adapted to the receiving language's sounds and morphology.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: How many morphemes occur in unhelpfulness under the ordinary analysis?
questions.explanation: The units are un- + help + -ful + -ness. Each contributes lexical or grammatical meaning. Syllable count and letter count answer different questions.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Choose the regular English plural ending sequence for cats, dogs and buses.
questions.explanation: A voiceless nonsibilant conditions [s], a voiced nonsibilant conditions [z], and a sibilant conditions a syllabic plural, commonly transcribed [ɪz] or [əz] depending on variety and analysis.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Choose the past-ending sequence for walked, played and wanted.
questions.explanation: Regular past tense has [t] after voiceless segments other than /t/, [d] after voiced segments other than /d/, and a syllabic form after /t/ or /d/.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: In the boy from China, what is the category of from China?
questions.explanation: From is the head, so the constituent is a prepositional phrase. It modifies a noun, but adjectival function does not change its head category.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which example is a clear adjective phrase by head category?
