questions.explanation: Proud heads very proud of her work. A proud student is a noun phrase, in a proud manner is a prepositional phrase, and She is proud is a clause.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which analysis of men is appropriate in introductory English morphology?
options: An ordinary infix -e- added to man.
A compound of two complete nouns.
An irregular plural involving internal vowel change.
questions.explanation: The plural relation involves a vowel alternation rather than an inserted affix. Its morphological analysis should not be confused with genuine infixation.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

options: The smallest unit with a meaning or grammatical function in a morphological analysis.
Every morpheme must be an entire written word.
A morpheme may be free or bound; grammatical meaning counts even without a concrete object referent.

questions.explanation:

The smallest unit with a meaning or grammatical function in a morphological analysis.
Example: Cats contains cat and a plural marker.

options: An observable form realizing a morpheme.

A morph is an abstract meaning with no realization.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A morph is an abstract meaning with no realization.”
An observable form realizing a morpheme.

options: An alternative realization of the same morpheme.

Allomorphs preserve the relevant grammatical contribution despite differences in form.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Alternative plural allomorphs must express different grammatical numbers.”
An alternative realization of the same morpheme.
Example: English regular plurals have [s], [z] and [ɪz] realizations.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Free morpheme is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Book can occur alone and also inside books.
A free morpheme must always attach to another morpheme.
A morpheme capable of occurring as a word on its own.
A complex word such as duster is not a single free morpheme merely because it can stand alone.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A free morpheme must always attach to another morpheme.”
A morpheme capable of occurring as a word on its own.
Example: Book can occur alone and also inside books.

questions.question: Which statement about Bound morpheme is INACCURATE?
options: Affixes are bound, but bound roots also occur, so bound morpheme and affix are not exact synonyms.
A morpheme that cannot ordinarily occur independently as a word.
An illustration is: The past-tense suffix -ed attaches to a verbal base.
Every bound morpheme is a complete independent sentence.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every bound morpheme is a complete independent sentence.”
A morpheme that cannot ordinarily occur independently as a word.
Example: The past-tense suffix -ed attaches to a verbal base.
Important distinction: Affixes are bound, but bound roots also occur, so bound morpheme and affix are not exact synonyms.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Lexical morpheme is INACCURATE?
options: A morpheme contributing substantial content meaning.
Lexical roots often belong to open classes such as nouns, verbs and adjectives.
An illustration is: The root tiger contributes the animal concept in tigers.
Lexical morphemes are restricted to articles and conjunctions.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Lexical morphemes are restricted to articles and conjunctions.”
A morpheme contributing substantial content meaning.
Example: The root tiger contributes the animal concept in tigers.

questions.question: Which statement about Functional morpheme is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: The article the marks a noun phrase as definite in a suitable context.
The category includes free function words and, in broader usage, bound grammatical markers.
A morpheme contributing grammatical organization or relational information.
Functional morphemes have no grammatical contribution at all.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Functional morphemes have no grammatical contribution at all.”
A morpheme contributing grammatical organization or relational information.
Example: The article the marks a noun phrase as definite in a suitable context.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Derivation is INACCURATE?
options: Derivation must always change the grammatical category of its base.
Morphology forming a new lexeme or a new lexical meaning, sometimes changing word class.
An illustration is: Adding un- to happy creates unhappy.
Unhappy remains an adjective; category preservation does not prevent an operation from being derivational.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Derivation must always change the grammatical category of its base.”
Morphology forming a new lexeme or a new lexical meaning, sometimes changing word class.
Example: Adding un- to happy creates unhappy.

questions.question: Which statement about Inflection is INACCURATE?
options: Morphology expressing grammatical contrasts within a lexeme's paradigm.

Inflection generally preserves lexical category and core lexical identity.
English past-tense inflection always creates a new noun lexeme.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “English past-tense inflection always creates a new noun lexeme.”
Morphology expressing grammatical contrasts within a lexeme's paradigm.
Example: Walk and walked express different grammatical forms of the same verb.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Prefix is INACCURATE?
options: Position defines a prefix; whether it is derivational or inflectional depends on its function in the language.
An illustration is: Re- precedes write in rewrite.
An affix attached before its base.
A prefix must occur after the root.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A prefix must occur after the root.”
An affix attached before its base.
Example: Re- precedes write in rewrite.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Suffix is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: -ness follows kind in kindness.
An affix attached after its base.
A suffix must be inserted in the middle of a root.
English suffixes can be derivational or inflectional, as -ness and plural -s illustrate.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A suffix must be inserted in the middle of a root.”
An affix attached after its base.
Example: -ness follows kind in kindness.
Important distinction: English suffixes can be derivational or inflectional, as -ness and plural -s illustrate.

questions.question: Which statement about Infix is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Tagalog sulat and sumulat illustrate an inserted -um-.
The English plural men is formed by inserting an ordinary infix into man.
An affix inserted within a root or base.
Men illustrates internal vowel change; genuine infixation requires an inserted morphological element.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “The English plural men is formed by inserting an ordinary infix into man.”

questions.question: Which statement about Root is INACCURATE?
options: Roots can be free or bound; not every root can occur as an independent word.

The basic lexical core remaining after relevant affixes are removed.
A root is always the final inflectional ending of a word.

The inaccurate claim is: “A root is always the final inflectional ending of a word.”
The basic lexical core remaining after relevant affixes are removed.
Example: Help is the root in unhelpfulness.
Important distinction: Roots can be free or bound; not every root can occur as an independent word.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Base is INACCURATE?
options: A base must contain exactly one morpheme.
A base may be a root or an already complex form.
A form to which a morphological operation applies.

A form to which a morphological operation applies.

questions.question: Which statement about Stem is INACCURATE?
options: A stem can never contain a derivational suffix.
A form to which an inflectional operation applies in a common introductory usage.
An illustration is: Worker is the stem receiving plural -s in workers.
Stem and base terminology varies somewhat across frameworks; the intended definition should be stated.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A stem can never contain a derivational suffix.”
A form to which an inflectional operation applies in a common introductory usage.
Example: Worker is the stem receiving plural -s in workers.
Important distinction: Stem and base terminology varies somewhat across frameworks; the intended definition should be stated.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Regular plural allomorphy is INACCURATE?
options: A sibilant requires the syllabic variant; otherwise the preceding segment's voicing normally conditions the ending.
An illustration is: Dogs ends in [z], cats in [s], and buses in [ɪz] in many descriptions.
The plural ending in dogs is normally the same voiceless [s] as in cats.
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English plural ending.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “The plural ending in dogs is normally the same voiceless [s] as in cats.”
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English plural ending.
Example: Dogs ends in [z], cats in [s], and buses in [ɪz] in many descriptions.
Important distinction: A sibilant requires the syllabic variant; otherwise the preceding segment's voicing normally conditions the ending.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Regular past allomorphy is INACCURATE?
options: Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English past-tense ending.
An illustration is: Walked has [t], played [d], and wanted [ɪd] in common transcriptions.
Every written -ed ending necessarily forms a separate syllable.
The syllabic variant follows /t/ or /d/; other environments condition [t] or [d].
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every written -ed ending necessarily forms a separate syllable.”
Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English past-tense ending.
Example: Walked has [t], played [d], and wanted [ɪd] in common transcriptions.
Important distinction: The syllabic variant follows /t/ or /d/; other environments condition [t] or [d].

questions.question: Which statement about Suppletion is INACCURATE?
options: A morphological relation involving forms with substantially different roots.

Suppletion is merely adding regular -ed to every verb.
The relation is grammatical despite the absence of an ordinary predictable shared root shape.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Suppletion is merely adding regular -ed to every verb.”
A morphological relation involving forms with substantially different roots.
Example: Go and went are related as present and past forms of one verb.
Important distinction: The relation is grammatical despite the absence of an ordinary predictable shared root shape.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Zero plural is INACCURATE?
options: Number can be identified from syntax and context even when the noun has no overt plural marker.
A noun without a visible suffix can never be plural.
An illustration is: One sheep and three sheep share the same overt noun form.
A plural form without an overt plural affix in an appropriate analysis.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A noun without a visible suffix can never be plural.”
A plural form without an overt plural affix in an appropriate analysis.

questions.question: Which statement about Internal vowel change is INACCURATE?
options: A morphological pattern realized by changing a vowel inside a base.

Internal modification differs from concatenating a separate prefix or suffix.
Internal vowel change requires a detachable infix in every case.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Internal vowel change requires a detachable infix in every case.”
A morphological pattern realized by changing a vowel inside a base.
Example: Sing, sang and sung differ in their internal vowels.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Compounding is INACCURATE?
options: Formation of a word from two or more lexical bases.
Spacing and hyphenation do not reliably determine compound status on their own.
An illustration is: Toothbrush combines tooth and brush.
A compound must be written as one uninterrupted string in every case.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A compound must be written as one uninterrupted string in every case.”
Formation of a word from two or more lexical bases.
Example: Toothbrush combines tooth and brush.
Important distinction: Spacing and hyphenation do not reliably determine compound status on their own.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Conversion is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: The noun bottle is used as a verb in They bottle the juice.
Also called zero derivation in some accounts, this process requires attention to actual use and analysis.
A change in lexical category without an overt derivational affix.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Conversion always requires the suffix -ness.”
A change in lexical category without an overt derivational affix.

questions.question: Which statement about Morpheme count is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Unhelpful contains three units: un-, help and -ful.
Teacher has two morphemes, while some multisyllabic words such as banana are monomorphemic.
The number of morphemes must equal the number of syllables.
The number of meaningful or grammatical units identified in a word.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “The number of morphemes must equal the number of syllables.”
The number of meaningful or grammatical units identified in a word.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Derivation before inflection is INACCURATE?
options: Morphological hierarchy matters; this English tendency should not be universalized without qualification.
A common English ordering in which derivation is nearer the root than outer inflection.
Workers is normally built by adding agentive -er outside already plural works.
An illustration is: Workers has work + -er + plural -s.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Workers is normally built by adding agentive -er outside already plural works.”
A common English ordering in which derivation is nearer the root than outer inflection.
Example: Workers has work + -er + plural -s.
Important distinction: Morphological hierarchy matters; this English tendency should not be universalized without qualification.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Noun phrase is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: The very old house functions as subject in The very old house collapsed.
A single noun or pronoun can form a phrase; determiner-phrase analyses provide a different theoretical treatment.
A noun phrase must always contain at least two written words.
A phrase headed by a noun or nominal element in a traditional introductory analysis.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A noun phrase must always contain at least two written words.”
A phrase headed by a noun or nominal element in a traditional introductory analysis.
Example: The very old house functions as subject in The very old house collapsed.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Prepositional phrase is INACCURATE?
options: A phrase headed by a preposition, often with a complement.
A phrase headed by under becomes an adjective phrase merely because it modifies a noun.
An illustration is: Under the table contains the preposition under and its complement.
Phrase category follows the head; grammatical function and phrase category must be distinguished.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A phrase headed by under becomes an adjective phrase merely because it modifies a noun.”
A phrase headed by a preposition, often with a complement.
Example: Under the table contains the preposition under and its complement.
Important distinction: Phrase category follows the head; grammatical function and phrase category must be distinguished.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Adjective phrase is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Very proud of her work is headed by proud.
Nice blue shirt is an adjective phrase headed by shirt.
Nice blue shirt is a noun phrase; adjective modifiers do not change its nominal head.
A phrase headed by an adjective.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Nice blue shirt is an adjective phrase headed by shirt.”
A phrase headed by an adjective.
Example: Very proud of her work is headed by proud.

questions.question: Which statement about Adverb phrase is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Quite slowly is headed by slowly.
In a loud voice is an adverb phrase by head category.
In a loud voice is a prepositional phrase that may function as an adverbial.
A phrase headed by an adverb.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “In a loud voice is an adverb phrase by head category.”
A phrase headed by an adverb.
Example: Quite slowly is headed by slowly.

questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Verb phrase is INACCURATE?
options: A phrase headed by a verb, with its dependents according to the framework used.

Every account limits a verb phrase to auxiliaries and excludes objects.
Some school grammars use a narrower verb-group label; state the adopted framework when boundaries matter.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every account limits a verb phrase to auxiliaries and excludes objects.”
A phrase headed by a verb, with its dependents according to the framework used.
Example: Has eaten the apple includes a verbal head and its object in a common syntactic analysis.
Important distinction: Some school grammars use a narrower verb-group label; state the adopted framework when boundaries matter.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Infinitival construction is INACCURATE?
options: Infinitival to always functions as a preposition taking a noun object.
An illustration is: To read novels functions as the complement of likes in She likes to read novels.
A nonfinite construction based on an infinitive verb.
Many modern grammars treat such units as nonfinite clauses rather than simply infinitive phrases.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Infinitival to always functions as a preposition taking a noun object.”
A nonfinite construction based on an infinitive verb.
Example: To read novels functions as the complement of likes in She likes to read novels.
Important distinction: Many modern grammars treat such units as nonfinite clauses rather than simply infinitive phrases.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Gerund construction is INACCURATE?
options: A nonfinite -ing construction traditionally associated with a nominal function.
An illustration is: Reading novels is relaxing places reading novels in subject position.
Compare a progressive verb in is reading; modern analyses often use a unified gerund-participial category.
Every word ending in -ing is a gerund functioning as a noun.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every word ending in -ing is a gerund functioning as a noun.”
A nonfinite -ing construction traditionally associated with a nominal function.
Example: Reading novels is relaxing places reading novels in subject position.
Important distinction: Compare a progressive verb in is reading; modern analyses often use a unified gerund-participial category.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Participial modifier is INACCURATE?
options: Restrictive modifiers often lack commas; supplementary participial constructions are commonly set off.
An illustration is: The child wearing a red hat waved uses wearing a red hat to modify child.
A participial construction modifying a nominal expression or supplying supplementary information.
Every participial modifier must be enclosed in commas.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every participial modifier must be enclosed in commas.”
A participial construction modifying a nominal expression or supplying supplementary information.
Example: The child wearing a red hat waved uses wearing a red hat to modify child.
Important distinction: Restrictive modifiers often lack commas; supplementary participial constructions are commonly set off.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Absolute construction is INACCURATE?
options: The construction comments on the accompanying situation; her eyes and on the clock form its internal relation.
A supplementary construction with its own subject-like element, often without a finite verb.
An absolute construction must always contain a finite past-tense verb.
An illustration is: Her eyes on the clock, Sara waited for the bus.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “An absolute construction must always contain a finite past-tense verb.”
A supplementary construction with its own subject-like element, often without a finite verb.
Example: Her eyes on the clock, Sara waited for the bus.
Important distinction: The construction comments on the accompanying situation; her eyes and on the clock form its internal relation.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Independent clause is INACCURATE?
options: Every clause introduced by although is independent.
Independence concerns syntactic status, not whether a reader needs any wider context to understand a reference.
An illustration is: Tara ate a cheese roll can stand independently.
A clause capable of functioning as a complete sentence in ordinary use.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every clause introduced by although is independent.”
A clause capable of functioning as a complete sentence in ordinary use.
Example: Tara ate a cheese roll can stand independently.
Important distinction: Independence concerns syntactic status, not whether a reader needs any wider context to understand a reference.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Dependent clause is INACCURATE?
options: A clause syntactically subordinate to another construction.
Finite subordinate clauses often have an overt subject and verb, while nonfinite clauses may omit an overt subject.
An illustration is: After she watched the news is subordinate in Tara ate after she watched the news.
A dependent clause must lack a verb.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A dependent clause must lack a verb.”
A clause syntactically subordinate to another construction.
Example: After she watched the news is subordinate in Tara ate after she watched the news.
Important distinction: Finite subordinate clauses often have an overt subject and verb, while nonfinite clauses may omit an overt subject.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Grammatical rank scale is INACCURATE?
options: A hierarchy of grammatical units in a stated framework.
Syntax names a field or level of analysis, not a unit equivalent to sentence on this scale.
Syntax itself is a grammatical unit on the same rank scale as word.
An illustration is: Sentence, clause, phrase, word and morpheme are arranged from larger to smaller units in an introductory scale.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Syntax itself is a grammatical unit on the same rank scale as word.”
A hierarchy of grammatical units in a stated framework.
Example: Sentence, clause, phrase, word and morpheme are arranged from larger to smaller units in an introductory scale.
Important distinction: Syntax names a field or level of analysis, not a unit equivalent to sentence on this scale.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Open lexical class is INACCURATE?
options: Openness is a tendency; nouns, verbs and adjectives are common examples.
An open lexical class is defined by being unable to gain new words.
An illustration is: English gains new nouns and verbs for new technologies.
A word class that readily admits new members.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “An open lexical class is defined by being unable to gain new words.”
A word class that readily admits new members.
Example: English gains new nouns and verbs for new technologies.
Important distinction: Openness is a tendency; nouns, verbs and adjectives are common examples.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Closed lexical class is INACCURATE?
options: A closed class can never change in any way over historical time.
An illustration is: English personal pronouns form a comparatively restricted inventory.
Closed means comparatively resistant to expansion, not eternally frozen.
A word class with relatively limited membership and limited ready addition.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A closed class can never change in any way over historical time.”
A word class with relatively limited membership and limited ready addition.
Example: English personal pronouns form a comparatively restricted inventory.
Important distinction: Closed means comparatively resistant to expansion, not eternally frozen.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about English inflection inventory is INACCURATE?
options: The conventional introductory list of eight English inflectional suffix categories.
An illustration is: Plural, possessive, third-person singular, past tense, two participles, comparative and superlative are listed.
Comparative -er in taller is inflectional; the similar-looking agentive -er is derivational.
Agentive -er in teacher belongs to the eight ordinary English inflectional suffix categories.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Agentive -er in teacher belongs to the eight ordinary English inflectional suffix categories.”
The conventional introductory list of eight English inflectional suffix categories.
Example: Plural, possessive, third-person singular, past tense, two participles, comparative and superlative are listed.
Important distinction: Comparative -er in taller is inflectional; the similar-looking agentive -er is derivational.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Blending is INACCURATE?
options: Blending requires retaining both complete words in every case.
It differs from ordinary compounding in which whole lexical bases are combined.
An illustration is: Brunch combines parts of breakfast and lunch.
Forming a word by combining portions of existing words.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Blending requires retaining both complete words in every case.”
Forming a word by combining portions of existing words.
Example: Brunch combines parts of breakfast and lunch.
Important distinction: It differs from ordinary compounding in which whole lexical bases are combined.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Clipping is INACCURATE?
options: Clipping requires adding a new derivational suffix.
An illustration is: Exam is a shortened form of examination.
Shortening does not necessarily change the word's core referential meaning or category.
Forming a shorter lexical form by shortening an existing word.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Clipping requires adding a new derivational suffix.”
Forming a shorter lexical form by shortening an existing word.
Example: Exam is a shortened form of examination.
Important distinction: Shortening does not necessarily change the word's core referential meaning or category.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Acronym formation is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: NASA is pronounced as a word rather than as a sequence of individual letter names.
Every initial-letter abbreviation must be pronounced as one word.
Terminology varies; the narrow contrast distinguishes acronyms from initialisms such as BBC.
Forming a word from initial letters that is pronounced as a word in a narrow usage.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every initial-letter abbreviation must be pronounced as one word.”
Forming a word from initial letters that is pronounced as a word in a narrow usage.
Example: NASA is pronounced as a word rather than as a sequence of individual letter names.
Important distinction: Terminology varies; the narrow contrast distinguishes acronyms from initialisms such as BBC.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which statement about Borrowing is INACCURATE?
options: Adoption of a linguistic form from another language.
An illustration is: English uses bungalow, historically borrowed from an Indian-language source.
Borrowings often become adapted to the receiving language's sounds and morphology.
A borrowed word must permanently retain every phonetic property of its source language.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A borrowed word must permanently retain every phonetic property of its source language.”
Adoption of a linguistic form from another language.
Example: English uses bungalow, historically borrowed from an Indian-language source.
Important distinction: Borrowings often become adapted to the receiving language's sounds and morphology.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which analysis of teachers is correct?
options: Tea + cher + s as three lexical roots.
questions.explanation: Agentive -er forms the noun teacher from teach, then plural -s inflects the derived noun. Comparative -er has a different grammatical function despite matching spelling.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which pair contains the same written suffix with different morphological functions?
questions.explanation: The -er of teacher forms an agent noun and is derivational; the -er of taller marks comparative degree and is inflectional. Matching orthography does not guarantee matching morphemes.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question: Which sentence contains a supplementary absolute construction?
options: Her eyes on the clock, Sara waited.
questions.explanation: Her eyes on the clock has its own nominal element and a predicative relation without a finite verb. It supplements the main clause rather than serving as its subject.
questions.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Internalized linguistic knowledge supporting a speaker's patterns and judgments.
questions.explanation:
Internalized linguistic knowledge supporting a speaker's patterns and judgments.
Example: A child uses word-order patterns without being able to state a school grammar rule.
Important distinction: Implicit knowledge is distinct from conscious terminology and explicit classroom instruction.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
An account of the patterns actually found in a language or variety.
questions.explanation:
An account of the patterns actually found in a language or variety.
Example: A grammar records a community's consistent use of multiple negation.
Important distinction: A nonstandard pattern can be systematic even when institutions discourage it.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Norms recommending which forms people should use in particular contexts.
questions.explanation:
Norms recommending which forms people should use in particular contexts.
Example: A style manual recommends a particular form for formal examination writing.
Important distinction: Prescriptions may be useful for a register, but they differ from a description of every variety.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
A grammar organized to support language teaching and learning.
questions.explanation:
A grammar organized to support language teaching and learning.
Example: A textbook explains English question formation with practice exercises.
Important distinction: It may simplify or sequence material, and need not compare the target language with a first language in every lesson.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A theoretical proposal about innate constraints or capacities specific to human language in generative approaches.
questions.explanation:
A theoretical proposal about innate constraints or capacities specific to human language in generative approaches.
Example: A generative account asks which aspects of possible grammars are biologically constrained.
Important distinction: The hypothesis and its scope are debated; it is not identical to any observed cross-linguistic generalization.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Conformity to the structural patterns of a specified language variety in an analysis.
questions.explanation:
Conformity to the structural patterns of a specified language variety in an analysis.
Example: The children are playing conforms to standard English agreement.
Important distinction: Grammaticality differs from truth, plausibility, politeness and stylistic preference.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Speakers' judgments of how natural or usable an expression seems in context.
questions.explanation:
Speakers' judgments of how natural or usable an expression seems in context.
Example: A highly nested sentence feels difficult despite following a proposed rule system.
Important distinction: Acceptability can reflect grammatical knowledge together with processing and contextual factors.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A theoretical separation of linguistic knowledge from its actual use.
questions.explanation:
A theoretical separation of linguistic knowledge from its actual use.
Example: A speaker knows a construction but produces a tired slip while saying it.
Important distinction: Performance data are evidence for competence, but interpretation must consider processing conditions.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
The inventory of lexical knowledge, including information about words and morphemes.
questions.explanation:
The inventory of lexical knowledge, including information about words and morphemes.
Example: A speaker knows that give typically permits a recipient and a theme.
Important distinction: Pronunciation, meaning and combinatorial properties may be part of lexical knowledge.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
The sound-related interface representation in generative models using the PF label.
questions.explanation:
The sound-related interface representation in generative models using the PF label.
Example: A derivation is interpreted on its pronunciation side at PF in a simplified model.
Important distinction: PF is a theoretical representation, not simply the visible written form of a sentence.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A meaning-related interface representation in generative models using the LF label.
questions.explanation:
A meaning-related interface representation in generative models using the LF label.
Example: A model uses LF to represent aspects of interpretation such as scope.
Important distinction: PF/LF terminology belongs to particular frameworks and should not be presented as a complete theory-neutral description.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Development of a linguistic system through experience and learning.
questions.explanation:
Development of a linguistic system through experience and learning.
Example: A child develops productive word combinations through interaction.
Important distinction: Broad developmental patterns coexist with substantial individual, linguistic and environmental variation.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Application of a productive pattern to a form that is irregular in adult usage.
questions.explanation:
Application of a productive pattern to a form that is irregular in adult usage.
Example: A child says goed where the adult form is went.
Important distinction: The error provides evidence for pattern generalization alongside learning of exceptional forms.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
Knowledge expressed in skilled use without necessarily being consciously verbalized.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge expressed in skilled use without necessarily being consciously verbalized.
Example: A fluent speaker chooses a natural word order but cannot explain the rule.
Important distinction: Explicit rule knowledge and fluent implicit performance can dissociate.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Consciously accessible knowledge that can be stated or reflected on.
questions.explanation:
Consciously accessible knowledge that can be stated or reflected on.
Example: A learner recites the rule for forming a regular English plural.
Important distinction: Explicit knowledge can support learning but does not automatically equal fluent performance.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
The linguistic principle that natural dialects are systematic rather than inherently deficient.
questions.explanation:
The linguistic principle that natural dialects are systematic rather than inherently deficient.
Example: A linguist treats regional agreement patterns as rule-governed.
Important distinction: Social opportunities associated with standard varieties are real, but do not establish structural superiority.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A socially established variety used in education, administration or other institutional settings.
questions.explanation:
A socially established variety used in education, administration or other institutional settings.
Example: A school adopts standard written English for examination essays.
Important distinction: Standardization is social and historical; other varieties also have structured linguistic systems.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
The linguistic patterns associated with an individual speaker.
questions.explanation:
The linguistic patterns associated with an individual speaker.
Example: One speaker consistently prefers a particular pronunciation and expression.
Important distinction: Individual patterns interact with community varieties and change across context and time.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Investigation of a linguistic system at a particular time or period.
questions.explanation:
Investigation of a linguistic system at a particular time or period.
Example: A study describes present-day Urdu case marking without tracing its history.
Important distinction: A synchronic description can involve variation; it does not mean every speaker uses identical forms.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
Investigation of linguistic change through time.
questions.explanation:
Investigation of linguistic change through time.
Example: A study traces the loss of certain English inflectional endings across centuries.
Important distinction: It concerns historical development, which differs from description at a single period.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
A proposed property or tendency holding across languages, stated with an appropriate scope.
questions.explanation:
A proposed property or tendency holding across languages, stated with an appropriate scope.
Example: A typologist tests whether a structural pattern occurs across a diverse language sample.
Important distinction: Absolute claims and statistical tendencies require different evidence and should not be conflated.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Comparison of structural patterns across languages.
questions.explanation:
Comparison of structural patterns across languages.
Example: Languages are compared according to their dominant ordering of subject, object and verb.
Important distinction: Typological grouping and genetic classification answer different questions.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
Observations drawn from systematically collected language data.
questions.explanation:
Observations drawn from systematically collected language data.
Example: Repeated corpus examples support the claim that a collocation is frequent in a register.
