questions.explanation: The cupboard drank the soup has familiar subject-verb-object order but assigns drinking to an inanimate item. Personification could make it interpretable in a special context.

questions.question: Which statement about Lexical semantics is INACCURATE?
options: The study of word and morpheme meanings and relations among lexical items.
Lexical semantics is restricted to meanings of entire paragraphs and excludes words.
Phrasal or compositional semantics instead investigates how larger meanings are built.
An illustration is: An analyst compares the meanings of couch and sofa.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Lexical semantics is restricted to meanings of entire paragraphs and excludes words.”
The study of word and morpheme meanings and relations among lexical items.
Example: An analyst compares the meanings of couch and sofa.
Important distinction: Phrasal or compositional semantics instead investigates how larger meanings are built.

questions.question: Which statement about Compositional semantics is INACCURATE?
options: The study of how complex meanings arise from constituent meanings and their combination.
An illustration is: The analyst explains the difference between Dog bites man and Man bites dog.
Word order and grammatical structure never affect sentence meaning.
The same words can yield different meanings when their structural relations change.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Word order and grammatical structure never affect sentence meaning.”
The study of how complex meanings arise from constituent meanings and their combination.
Example: The analyst explains the difference between Dog bites man and Man bites dog.
Important distinction: The same words can yield different meanings when their structural relations change.

questions.question: Which statement about Denotation is INACCURATE?
options: The entity or set of entities an expression applies to in a semantic interpretation.
An illustration is: In a suitable model, cat applies to the set of cats.
Denotation is simply any personal emotional association with a word.
Semantic denotations can be defined within models and need not be limited to objects currently visible.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Denotation is simply any personal emotional association with a word.”
The entity or set of entities an expression applies to in a semantic interpretation.
Example: In a suitable model, cat applies to the set of cats.
Important distinction: Semantic denotations can be defined within models and need not be limited to objects currently visible.

questions.question: Which statement about Connotation is INACCURATE?
options: Associated social, emotional or evaluative meaning connected with an expression.
Associations can vary across people, cultures and contexts, even when central descriptive meaning is shared.
Connotation is guaranteed to be identical for every speaker in every situation.
An illustration is: Home can evoke warmth or belonging beyond identifying a dwelling.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Connotation is guaranteed to be identical for every speaker in every situation.”
Associated social, emotional or evaluative meaning connected with an expression.
Example: Home can evoke warmth or belonging beyond identifying a dwelling.
Important distinction: Associations can vary across people, cultures and contexts, even when central descriptive meaning is shared.

questions.question: Which statement about Extension is INACCURATE?
options: The set of entities satisfying an expression in a specified world or situation.
An illustration is: The extension of student at a university includes the individuals enrolled there at the relevant time.
An expression's extension can never change when the world changes.
Membership can vary across worlds and times while the descriptive concept remains relatively stable.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “An expression's extension can never change when the world changes.”
The set of entities satisfying an expression in a specified world or situation.
Example: The extension of student at a university includes the individuals enrolled there at the relevant time.
Important distinction: Membership can vary across worlds and times while the descriptive concept remains relatively stable.

questions.question: Which statement about Intension is INACCURATE?
options: The descriptive content or rule determining an expression's extension across relevant situations or worlds.
An illustration is: Planet applies according to a concept rather than merely listing currently named objects.
Intension is exactly the same as a person's private emotional reaction to a word.
Intension differs from connotation; in formal semantics it is often modelled as a function from worlds to extensions.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Intension is exactly the same as a person's private emotional reaction to a word.”
The descriptive content or rule determining an expression's extension across relevant situations or worlds.
Example: Planet applies according to a concept rather than merely listing currently named objects.
Important distinction: Intension differs from connotation; in formal semantics it is often modelled as a function from worlds to extensions.

questions.question: Which statement about Conceptual meaning is INACCURATE?
options: Conceptual meaning consists only of a listener's fear of injections.
Fear is an association; descriptive features identify the intended sense of the expression.
The central descriptive content conventionally associated with an expression.
An illustration is: Needle is understood as a type of thin pointed implement in a relevant sense.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Conceptual meaning consists only of a listener's fear of injections.”
The central descriptive content conventionally associated with an expression.
Example: Needle is understood as a type of thin pointed implement in a relevant sense.
Important distinction: Fear is an association; descriptive features identify the intended sense of the expression.

questions.question: Which statement about Mental lexicon is INACCURATE?
options: A speaker's organized lexical knowledge, including forms, meanings and relevant grammatical properties.
An illustration is: A listener accesses a word's pronunciation and meaning during recognition.
It is a cognitive construct and need not be organized like a printed dictionary.
The mental lexicon contains only a list of alphabetically printed pages.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “The mental lexicon contains only a list of alphabetically printed pages.”
A speaker's organized lexical knowledge, including forms, meanings and relevant grammatical properties.
Example: A listener accesses a word's pronunciation and meaning during recognition.
Important distinction: It is a cognitive construct and need not be organized like a printed dictionary.

questions.question: Which statement about Semantic feature is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: An analysis distinguishes adult from child using an adulthood feature.
Every lexical meaning can always be exhaustively represented by a tiny fixed feature list.
Feature analysis is useful for selected contrasts but faces difficult cases and theory-dependent choices.
A component or property used to represent a meaning contrast.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every lexical meaning can always be exhaustively represented by a tiny fixed feature list.”
A component or property used to represent a meaning contrast.
Example: An analysis distinguishes adult from child using an adulthood feature.
Important distinction: Feature analysis is useful for selected contrasts but faces difficult cases and theory-dependent choices.

questions.question: Which statement about Semantic range is INACCURATE?
options: A word's semantic range proves that every one of its senses fits every context.
The range of senses or uses associated with a lexical item in a stated analysis.
An illustration is: Run appears in contexts about moving quickly, managing a shop and operating a machine.
Context and construction constrain which sense is intended.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A word's semantic range proves that every one of its senses fits every context.”
The range of senses or uses associated with a lexical item in a stated analysis.
Example: Run appears in contexts about moving quickly, managing a shop and operating a machine.
Important distinction: Context and construction constrain which sense is intended.

questions.question: Which statement about Selectional restriction is INACCURATE?
options: A semantic compatibility constraint or expectation on an expression's arguments.
A selectional anomaly is automatically a word-order error.
Metaphor, personification and special contexts can support interpretations that violate ordinary literal expectations.
An illustration is: The table drank tea is anomalous in an ordinary literal interpretation.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A selectional anomaly is automatically a word-order error.”
A semantic compatibility constraint or expectation on an expression's arguments.
Example: The table drank tea is anomalous in an ordinary literal interpretation.
Important distinction: Metaphor, personification and special contexts can support interpretations that violate ordinary literal expectations.

questions.question: Which statement about Synonymy is INACCURATE?
options: A relation of identical or close meaning in the relevant sense and context.
Synonymy is often partial; collocation, register and nuance may differ.
An illustration is: Couch and sofa are near synonyms for a type of seating.
Near synonyms must be interchangeable in every idiom and social register.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Near synonyms must be interchangeable in every idiom and social register.”
A relation of identical or close meaning in the relevant sense and context.
Example: Couch and sofa are near synonyms for a type of seating.
Important distinction: Synonymy is often partial; collocation, register and nuance may differ.

questions.question: Which statement about Antonymy is INACCURATE?
options: A broad relation of opposition in meaning.
Gradable, complementary and relational oppositions should be distinguished.
An illustration is: Hot and cold contrast along a temperature dimension.
All antonyms necessarily form a binary opposition with no intermediate cases.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “All antonyms necessarily form a binary opposition with no intermediate cases.”
A broad relation of opposition in meaning.
Example: Hot and cold contrast along a temperature dimension.
Important distinction: Gradable, complementary and relational oppositions should be distinguished.

questions.question: Which statement about Gradable opposition is INACCURATE?
options: Comparatives such as hotter and colder reflect the scalar nature of the contrast.
Not hot must always entail cold.
An opposition organized along a scale admitting intermediate values.
An illustration is: Something can be neither hot nor cold but warm.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Not hot must always entail cold.”
An opposition organized along a scale admitting intermediate values.
Example: Something can be neither hot nor cold but warm.
Important distinction: Comparatives such as hotter and colder reflect the scalar nature of the contrast.

questions.question: Which statement about Complementary opposition is INACCURATE?
options: A binary opposition in an idealized domain where one alternative excludes the other.
The domain and interpretation matter; borderline biological or figurative cases require qualification.
An illustration is: In an ordinary binary biological classification of an organism, alive contrasts with dead.
Every pair of complementary terms has a normal intermediate point on a degree scale.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every pair of complementary terms has a normal intermediate point on a degree scale.”
A binary opposition in an idealized domain where one alternative excludes the other.
Example: In an ordinary binary biological classification of an organism, alive contrasts with dead.
Important distinction: The domain and interpretation matter; borderline biological or figurative cases require qualification.

questions.question: Which statement about Relational converse is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: If A sold a book to B, B bought the book from A.
A relation in which opposed terms describe the same situation from different participant perspectives.
Converse relations reverse participant perspective rather than describing opposite temperatures on a scale.
Buy and sell describe two unrelated events whenever a transfer occurs.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Buy and sell describe two unrelated events whenever a transfer occurs.”
A relation in which opposed terms describe the same situation from different participant perspectives.
Example: If A sold a book to B, B bought the book from A.
Important distinction: Converse relations reverse participant perspective rather than describing opposite temperatures on a scale.

questions.question: Which statement about Homonymy is INACCURATE?
options: Distinguishing homonymy from polysemy can require historical and synchronic evidence.
Distinct lexical items sharing a form with unrelated meanings.
An illustration is: Bank meaning a financial institution and bank meaning a river edge share a form.
Every pair of related senses of one word must be homonymy.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every pair of related senses of one word must be homonymy.”
Distinct lexical items sharing a form with unrelated meanings.
Example: Bank meaning a financial institution and bank meaning a river edge share a form.
Important distinction: Distinguishing homonymy from polysemy can require historical and synchronic evidence.

questions.question: Which statement about Homophony is INACCURATE?
options: Homophony concerns sound; spelling identity is a separate issue.
Identity of pronunciation between distinct lexical items.
Homophones must always have identical spelling.
An illustration is: Flour and flower sound alike in many English varieties.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Homophones must always have identical spelling.”
Identity of pronunciation between distinct lexical items.
Example: Flour and flower sound alike in many English varieties.
Important distinction: Homophony concerns sound; spelling identity is a separate issue.

questions.question: Which statement about Homography is INACCURATE?
options: Identity of spelling between lexical items or forms, whether or not pronunciation matches.
Homographs must always be pronounced identically.
Homography concerns the written form; some homographs are also homophones.
An illustration is: Lead meaning guide and lead meaning the metal share spelling but differ in pronunciation.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Homographs must always be pronounced identically.”
Identity of spelling between lexical items or forms, whether or not pronunciation matches.
Example: Lead meaning guide and lead meaning the metal share spelling but differ in pronunciation.
Important distinction: Homography concerns the written form; some homographs are also homophones.

questions.question: Which statement about Polysemy is INACCURATE?
options: Relatedness of senses distinguishes the usual polysemy analysis from homonymy, though boundaries can be debated.
An illustration is: Head refers to a body part and also to the leader of an organization.
Multiple related senses associated with one lexical item.
Polysemy requires unrelated words with coincidentally matching forms.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Polysemy requires unrelated words with coincidentally matching forms.”
Multiple related senses associated with one lexical item.
Example: Head refers to a body part and also to the leader of an organization.
Important distinction: Relatedness of senses distinguishes the usual polysemy analysis from homonymy, though boundaries can be debated.

questions.question: Which statement about Hyponymy is INACCURATE?
options: A meaning relation in which one expression denotes a subtype of another.
An illustration is: Rose is a hyponym of flower.
If an entity is a rose, it is a flower, but the reverse implication does not generally hold.
Every flower must be a rose.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every flower must be a rose.”
A meaning relation in which one expression denotes a subtype of another.
Example: Rose is a hyponym of flower.
Important distinction: If an entity is a rose, it is a flower, but the reverse implication does not generally hold.

questions.question: Which statement about Hypernymy is INACCURATE?
options: A hypernym includes the subtype in its extension; its descriptive content is usually less specific.
A meaning relation in which one expression names a superordinate category.
An illustration is: Vehicle is a hypernym of bus.
Bus is more general than vehicle in the ordinary classification.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Bus is more general than vehicle in the ordinary classification.”
A meaning relation in which one expression names a superordinate category.
Example: Vehicle is a hypernym of bus.
Important distinction: A hypernym includes the subtype in its extension; its descriptive content is usually less specific.

questions.question: Which statement about Co-hyponymy is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Bus and car are co-hyponyms under vehicle.
Shared category membership does not make the subtypes identical in meaning.
A relation between subtypes sharing a superordinate category.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Co-hyponyms must always be synonyms.”
A relation between subtypes sharing a superordinate category.
Example: Bus and car are co-hyponyms under vehicle.
Important distinction: Shared category membership does not make the subtypes identical in meaning.

questions.question: Which statement about Meronymy is INACCURATE?
options: A wheel is a kind of car in the same way that a bus is a kind of vehicle.
An illustration is: Wheel is a meronym of car in the relevant part-whole sense.
Meronymy concerns parts; hyponymy concerns subtypes, so the relations are different.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A wheel is a kind of car in the same way that a bus is a kind of vehicle.”
A part-whole lexical relation.
Example: Wheel is a meronym of car in the relevant part-whole sense.
Important distinction: Meronymy concerns parts; hyponymy concerns subtypes, so the relations are different.

questions.question: Which statement about Metonymy is INACCURATE?
options: Reference through a salient association or contiguity between entities.
Metonymy always depends on a comparison of similar shapes.
Association such as institution-for-people distinguishes it from resemblance-based metaphor.
An illustration is: The White House announced a decision uses a building name for an institution or its officials.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Metonymy always depends on a comparison of similar shapes.”
Reference through a salient association or contiguity between entities.
Example: The White House announced a decision uses a building name for an institution or its officials.
Important distinction: Association such as institution-for-people distinguishes it from resemblance-based metaphor.

questions.question: Which statement about Metaphor is INACCURATE?
options: Interpretation of one domain or entity through another based on a perceived mapping or comparison.
Metaphorical interpretation draws on context and conceptual associations.
An illustration is: Calling a fierce competitor a tiger attributes qualities without literally identifying a species.
Every metaphor is an ordinary literal claim that two entities are biologically identical.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every metaphor is an ordinary literal claim that two entities are biologically identical.”
Interpretation of one domain or entity through another based on a perceived mapping or comparison.
Example: Calling a fierce competitor a tiger attributes qualities without literally identifying a species.
Important distinction: Metaphorical interpretation draws on context and conceptual associations.

questions.question: Which statement about Prototype is INACCURATE?
options: A particularly representative exemplar of a category for a person or community.
An illustration is: A robin may be judged a more typical bird than a penguin in some communities.
A less typical bird is therefore not a member of the bird category.
Typicality is graded and culturally variable; category membership and typicality are distinct.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A less typical bird is therefore not a member of the bird category.”
A particularly representative exemplar of a category for a person or community.
Example: A robin may be judged a more typical bird than a penguin in some communities.
Important distinction: Typicality is graded and culturally variable; category membership and typicality are distinct.

questions.question: Which statement about Lexical ambiguity is INACCURATE?
options: Availability of more than one interpretation due to the lexical senses or identities of a form.
Lexical ambiguity must always come from alternative phrase attachments.
An illustration is: I waited at the bank leaves open a financial or river-side interpretation without further context.
Context can disambiguate lexical items, while attachment ambiguity concerns structure.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Lexical ambiguity must always come from alternative phrase attachments.”
Availability of more than one interpretation due to the lexical senses or identities of a form.
Example: I waited at the bank leaves open a financial or river-side interpretation without further context.
Important distinction: Context can disambiguate lexical items, while attachment ambiguity concerns structure.

questions.question: Which statement about Agent is INACCURATE?
options: The agent must always be the grammatical subject, even in a passive.
An illustration is: Ali deliberately opened the door assigns Ali the agent role.
In The door was opened by Ali, Ali remains agent while the door is subject.
A semantic role typically associated with an intentional initiator of an action.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “The agent must always be the grammatical subject, even in a passive.”
A semantic role typically associated with an intentional initiator of an action.
Example: Ali deliberately opened the door assigns Ali the agent role.
Important distinction: In The door was opened by Ali, Ali remains agent while the door is subject.

questions.question: Which statement about Theme is INACCURATE?
options: Theme always means the intentional human initiator of an event.
A semantic role for an entity undergoing movement, change or a relevant state in a given analysis.
An illustration is: The book moves in Sara carried the book upstairs.
Some frameworks distinguish patient from theme more narrowly; role inventories vary.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Theme always means the intentional human initiator of an event.”
A semantic role for an entity undergoing movement, change or a relevant state in a given analysis.
Example: The book moves in Sara carried the book upstairs.
Important distinction: Some frameworks distinguish patient from theme more narrowly; role inventories vary.

questions.question: Which statement about Experiencer is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Sara is the experiencer in Sara fears spiders.
An experiencer must intentionally cause the emotion experienced.
A semantic role for a participant who perceives, feels or has a mental state.
Experiencers need not control their state and are distinct from intentional agents.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “An experiencer must intentionally cause the emotion experienced.”
A semantic role for a participant who perceives, feels or has a mental state.
Example: Sara is the experiencer in Sara fears spiders.
Important distinction: Experiencers need not control their state and are distinct from intentional agents.

questions.question: Which statement about Instrument is INACCURATE?
options: A semantic role for the means used to carry out an action.
A participant used as a means differs from an agent initiating the action.
Instrument refers to the destination of a movement event.
An illustration is: A key is the instrument in Ali opened the door with a key.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Instrument refers to the destination of a movement event.”
A semantic role for the means used to carry out an action.
Example: A key is the instrument in Ali opened the door with a key.
Important distinction: A participant used as a means differs from an agent initiating the action.

questions.question: Which statement about Location is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: In Lahore supplies location in Sara worked in Lahore.
Source and goal concern origin and destination, while location concerns where something is situated.
A semantic role identifying where a state or event occurs.
Location necessarily describes the point of origin of every movement.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Location necessarily describes the point of origin of every movement.”
A semantic role identifying where a state or event occurs.
Example: In Lahore supplies location in Sara worked in Lahore.
Important distinction: Source and goal concern origin and destination, while location concerns where something is situated.

questions.question: Which statement about Source and goal is INACCURATE?
options: The roles distinguish direction even when neither expression is the grammatical subject.
An illustration is: From Lahore is source and to Karachi is goal in The parcel travelled from Lahore to Karachi.
Semantic roles identifying a movement's origin and destination respectively.
Source and goal always identify the same endpoint by definition.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Source and goal always identify the same endpoint by definition.”
Semantic roles identifying a movement's origin and destination respectively.
Example: From Lahore is source and to Karachi is goal in The parcel travelled from Lahore to Karachi.
Important distinction: The roles distinguish direction even when neither expression is the grammatical subject.

questions.question: Which statement about Possessor and cause is INACCURATE?
options: Cause is often called causer; some inventories include natural forces under a broader agent label.
Semantic roles identifying ownership and nonintentional causal contribution, respectively.
A natural force must be an intentional human agent whenever it causes a change.
An illustration is: Ali has a bicycle assigns a possessor; The wind broke the branch assigns a natural cause.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A natural force must be an intentional human agent whenever it causes a change.”
Semantic roles identifying ownership and nonintentional causal contribution, respectively.
Example: Ali has a bicycle assigns a possessor; The wind broke the branch assigns a natural cause.
Important distinction: Cause is often called causer; some inventories include natural forces under a broader agent label.

questions.question: Which statement about Entailment is INACCURATE?
options: Entailment is a truth-based relation, unlike a defeasible conversational suggestion.
An illustration is: Sara owns a red car entails that Sara owns a car.
A relation where the truth of one proposition guarantees another's truth under the intended interpretation.
An entailment may be cancelled while keeping the original proposition true in the same interpretation.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “An entailment may be cancelled while keeping the original proposition true in the same interpretation.”
A relation where the truth of one proposition guarantees another's truth under the intended interpretation.
Example: Sara owns a red car entails that Sara owns a car.
Important distinction: Entailment is a truth-based relation, unlike a defeasible conversational suggestion.

questions.question: Which statement about Contradiction is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Ali is asleep and Ali is not asleep conflict when time and intended sense are held fixed.
Hold reference, time and meaning constant before diagnosing a contradiction.
Any two sentences with different words must contradict one another.
Incompatibility between propositions that cannot both be true in the same relevant interpretation.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Any two sentences with different words must contradict one another.”
Incompatibility between propositions that cannot both be true in the same relevant interpretation.
Example: Ali is asleep and Ali is not asleep conflict when time and intended sense are held fixed.
Important distinction: Hold reference, time and meaning constant before diagnosing a contradiction.

questions.question: Which statement about Tautology is INACCURATE?
options: Logical truth differs from ordinary factual truth; pragmatic use can still make a tautology informative in context.
A proposition true by its logical form in the intended classical analysis.
A tautology is defined as an empirical weather prediction that may turn out false.
An illustration is: It is raining or it is not raining exemplifies excluded middle in classical logic.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A tautology is defined as an empirical weather prediction that may turn out false.”
A proposition true by its logical form in the intended classical analysis.
Example: It is raining or it is not raining exemplifies excluded middle in classical logic.
Important distinction: Logical truth differs from ordinary factual truth; pragmatic use can still make a tautology informative in context.

questions.question: Which statement about Sense is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Morning star and evening star differ in sense even when both refer to Venus.
Co-reference does not require identical descriptive or cognitive content.
An expression's linguistic meaning and its relations within a language, distinguished from particular reference.
Two expressions with the same referent must have identical sense.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Two expressions with the same referent must have identical sense.”
An expression's linguistic meaning and its relations within a language, distinguished from particular reference.
Example: Morning star and evening star differ in sense even when both refer to Venus.
Important distinction: Co-reference does not require identical descriptive or cognitive content.

questions.question: Which statement about Reference is INACCURATE?
options: The use of an expression to identify an entity in context.
Reference is identical to every emotional association a hearer has with a word.
An illustration is: A speaker uses that student to identify a particular person in the room.
Referential interpretation draws on linguistic meaning and contextual information.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Reference is identical to every emotional association a hearer has with a word.”
The use of an expression to identify an entity in context.
Example: A speaker uses that student to identify a particular person in the room.
Important distinction: Referential interpretation draws on linguistic meaning and contextual information.

questions.question: Which statement about Analytic statement is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Every bachelor is unmarried is an introductory example using the ordinary adult-person sense.
Examples depend on the stipulated sense; social and institutional uses can complicate apparently simple definitions.
A statement true in virtue of meanings under an adopted semantic analysis.
An analytic statement is defined as one requiring a survey to discover whether its words mean what they do.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “An analytic statement is defined as one requiring a survey to discover whether its words mean what they do.”
A statement true in virtue of meanings under an adopted semantic analysis.
Example: Every bachelor is unmarried is an introductory example using the ordinary adult-person sense.
Important distinction: Examples depend on the stipulated sense; social and institutional uses can complicate apparently simple definitions.

questions.question: Which classification best fits The university decided to increase fees, when university refers to decision-makers?
options: Literal identification of a building's mental state.
questions.explanation: An institution label stands for its authorized people or decision-making body through association. This differs from a metaphor based primarily on cross-domain comparison.

questions.question: A penguin is judged less typical than a sparrow as a bird. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: A penguin is therefore not a bird.
Typicality and category membership can differ.
All category members must be equally typical.
The words penguin and bird are antonyms.
questions.explanation: Prototype judgments rank representativeness, not necessarily membership. Penguins remain birds despite departing from some familiar expectations such as flight.

questions.question: Morning star and evening star refer to Venus but present it differently. What does this show?
options: Every co-referring expression is a homophone.
Same reference need not mean same sense.
Same reference guarantees identical descriptive content.
Reference depends only on spelling length.
questions.explanation: The example distinguishes what an expression refers to from its sense or mode of presentation. A referent alone does not exhaust every aspect of meaning.

questions.question: Sara owns a red car, but she does not own a car is inconsistent in the ordinary sense. Why?
options: Red car and car are unrelated homonyms.
The first clause entails the proposition denied by the second.
Ownership is a type of phonetic aspiration.
The first clause merely suggests a cancellable social greeting.
questions.explanation: The red-car proposition guarantees car ownership under the stated reading. Denying that consequence creates a contradiction, unlike cancelling an ordinary conversational implicature.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
The message or intention a speaker communicates in a particular use.
questions.explanation:
The message or intention a speaker communicates in a particular use.
Example: A teacher says It is noisy here to encourage the class to quieten down.
Important distinction: Interpreting an intention uses the utterance plus evidence about context; it is not unrestricted mind-reading.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
The surrounding language that supports interpretation of an expression.
questions.explanation:
The surrounding language that supports interpretation of an expression.
Example: In Sara bought a book. She read it, preceding expressions help interpret she and it.
Important distinction: Also called co-text, it differs from physical and wider social circumstances.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Relevant features of the communicative situation and shared background.
questions.explanation:
Relevant features of the communicative situation and shared background.
Example: A warning about a coming car is interpreted differently beside a road than in a delivery discussion.
Important distinction: Participants, place, time, purposes and assumed background can all affect interpretation.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.
Information participants treat as shared for the purposes of their interaction.
questions.explanation:
Information participants treat as shared for the purposes of their interaction.
Example: Two colleagues refer to the meeting because both know which scheduled meeting is relevant.
Important distinction: Shared assumptions can be local to an interaction and can be mistaken or negotiated.

questions.question:
Which concept is defined by the following description?
A defeasible meaning inferred from an utterance and conversational reasoning beyond what is explicitly said.
questions.explanation:
A defeasible meaning inferred from an utterance and conversational reasoning beyond what is explicitly said.
Example: Some students passed may suggest not all, though the speaker can add in fact all did.
Important distinction: Implicatures depend on contextual assumptions and can often be cancelled without contradiction.

questions.question:
Which term best matches this definition?
Grice's framework for reasoning about contributions appropriate to an accepted conversational purpose.
questions.explanation:
Grice's framework for reasoning about contributions appropriate to an accepted conversational purpose.
Example: A listener interprets an apparently indirect reply as relevant to the ongoing discussion.
Important distinction: It is an interpretive framework, not a claim that every actual conversation is morally cooperative.

questions.question:
Identify the concept described below.

A conversational expectation favoring clarity, order and avoidance of obscurity or unnecessary ambiguity.
Example: A speaker gives ordered directions in clear language.
Important distinction: Manner concerns how something is expressed; evidential truthfulness belongs to quality.

questions.question: Which statement about Flouting a maxim is INACCURATE?
options: An overt apparent failure to satisfy a maxim that invites an additional interpretation.
A conspicuous mismatch can prompt implicature; flouting differs from covert violation.
Flouting is defined as secretly deceiving the listener without any recoverable signal.
An illustration is: During heavy rain, a speaker says Lovely weather! with an obviously ironic delivery.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Flouting is defined as secretly deceiving the listener without any recoverable signal.”
An overt apparent failure to satisfy a maxim that invites an additional interpretation.
Example: During heavy rain, a speaker says Lovely weather! with an obviously ironic delivery.
Important distinction: A conspicuous mismatch can prompt implicature; flouting differs from covert violation.

questions.question: Which statement about Violating a maxim is INACCURATE?
options: A covert failure to satisfy a conversational maxim, potentially misleading the listener.
An illustration is: Someone knowingly gives a false alibi while intending it to be believed.
Whether a maxim is flouted or violated depends on the interaction and the speaker's apparent communicative stance.
Every violation is a transparent invitation to infer irony.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every violation is a transparent invitation to infer irony.”
A covert failure to satisfy a conversational maxim, potentially misleading the listener.
Example: Someone knowingly gives a false alibi while intending it to be believed.
Important distinction: Whether a maxim is flouted or violated depends on the interaction and the speaker's apparent communicative stance.

questions.question: Which statement about Locutionary act is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: A speaker utters The gate is open with its ordinary sentence meaning.
Locutionary act means only the psychological effect on a frightened listener.
Producing an utterance with a linguistic form and propositional meaning in speech-act analysis.
Locution concerns saying something; illocution concerns the act performed in saying it.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Locutionary act means only the psychological effect on a frightened listener.”
Producing an utterance with a linguistic form and propositional meaning in speech-act analysis.
Example: A speaker utters The gate is open with its ordinary sentence meaning.
Important distinction: Locution concerns saying something; illocution concerns the act performed in saying it.

questions.question: Which statement about Illocutionary act is INACCURATE?
options: Illocutionary force is identical to the physical volume of the voice.
An illustration is: Saying The gate is open functions as a warning that a child may leave.
The same sentence can perform different acts in different contexts.
The communicative act performed in saying something, such as warning, requesting or promising.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Illocutionary force is identical to the physical volume of the voice.”
The communicative act performed in saying something, such as warning, requesting or promising.
Example: Saying The gate is open functions as a warning that a child may leave.
Important distinction: The same sentence can perform different acts in different contexts.

questions.question: Which statement about Perlocutionary effect is INACCURATE?
options: Intended communicative act and actual consequence differ; an appropriate warning may fail to persuade.
A warning has no illocutionary force unless the listener actually becomes afraid.
An illustration is: A warning causes a listener to move away from a road.
An effect of an utterance on a hearer's actions, feelings or beliefs.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A warning has no illocutionary force unless the listener actually becomes afraid.”
An effect of an utterance on a hearer's actions, feelings or beliefs.
Example: A warning causes a listener to move away from a road.
Important distinction: Intended communicative act and actual consequence differ; an appropriate warning may fail to persuade.

questions.question: Which statement about Direct speech act is INACCURATE?
options: An act whose typical communicative function aligns with the conventional function of its clause form.
An illustration is: Close the door is used straightforwardly to command closure.
Directness concerns the relation between form and function, not merely whether a verb is explicitly named.
A direct speech act must contain a performative verb such as promise.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A direct speech act must contain a performative verb such as promise.”
An act whose typical communicative function aligns with the conventional function of its clause form.
Example: Close the door is used straightforwardly to command closure.
Important distinction: Directness concerns the relation between form and function, not merely whether a verb is explicitly named.

questions.question: Which statement about Indirect speech act is INACCURATE?
options: An act communicated through a form conventionally associated with another function.
Listeners infer the intended act from conventions, context and background assumptions.
An illustration is: Could you pass the salt? is used as a request rather than a test of physical ability.
Every interrogative utterance can function only as a request for information.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every interrogative utterance can function only as a request for information.”
An act communicated through a form conventionally associated with another function.
Example: Could you pass the salt? is used as a request rather than a test of physical ability.
Important distinction: Listeners infer the intended act from conventions, context and background assumptions.

questions.question: Which statement about Explicit performative is INACCURATE?
options: An utterance that explicitly names the act it performs in appropriate circumstances.
First-person present use is a common pattern, but felicity and actual communicative use also matter.
The past report I promised yesterday necessarily makes a new promise now.
An illustration is: I promise to return the book tomorrow names the commitment being made.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “The past report I promised yesterday necessarily makes a new promise now.”
An utterance that explicitly names the act it performs in appropriate circumstances.
Example: I promise to return the book tomorrow names the commitment being made.
Important distinction: First-person present use is a common pattern, but felicity and actual communicative use also matter.

questions.question: Which statement about Felicity conditions is INACCURATE?
options: Conditions required for a speech act to be appropriate or successful in a relevant sense.
An illustration is: An institutional declaration succeeds only when authority and procedures are appropriate.
Any institutional formula works equally well when spoken by an unauthorized passer-by.
Conditions differ across acts and may concern authority, circumstances, sincerity and commitment.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Any institutional formula works equally well when spoken by an unauthorized passer-by.”
Conditions required for a speech act to be appropriate or successful in a relevant sense.
Example: An institutional declaration succeeds only when authority and procedures are appropriate.
Important distinction: Conditions differ across acts and may concern authority, circumstances, sincerity and commitment.

questions.question: Which statement about Assertive is INACCURATE?
options: Assertions and reports concern truth commitment, while directives seek action from a hearer.
A speech-act class committing the speaker to the truth of a proposition.
An illustration is: A witness states that the door was locked.
An assertive is defined solely as an attempt to get someone else to act.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “An assertive is defined solely as an attempt to get someone else to act.”
A speech-act class committing the speaker to the truth of a proposition.
Example: A witness states that the door was locked.
Important distinction: Assertions and reports concern truth commitment, while directives seek action from a hearer.

questions.question: Which statement about Directive is INACCURATE?
options: A speech-act class aiming to get an addressee to do something.
A directive necessarily commits the speaker to a future action of their own.
Requests and commands are directives; speaker commitments characterize commissives.
An illustration is: A teacher asks the class to open their books.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A directive necessarily commits the speaker to a future action of their own.”
A speech-act class aiming to get an addressee to do something.
Example: A teacher asks the class to open their books.
Important distinction: Requests and commands are directives; speaker commitments characterize commissives.

questions.question: Which statement about Commissive is INACCURATE?
options: Promises and some offers commit a speaker, subject to the context and the act's conditions.
A speech-act class committing the speaker to a future course of action.
Commissives only describe the present temperature.
An illustration is: A student promises to submit the assignment tomorrow.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Commissives only describe the present temperature.”
A speech-act class committing the speaker to a future course of action.
Example: A student promises to submit the assignment tomorrow.
Important distinction: Promises and some offers commit a speaker, subject to the context and the act's conditions.

questions.question: Which statement about Expressive is INACCURATE?
options: Apologies and congratulations express attitudes; declarations require a different institutional relation.
A speech-act class expressing an attitude or psychological state about a situation.
Every expressive changes a person's legal status through institutional authority.
An illustration is: A speaker apologizes for arriving late.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every expressive changes a person's legal status through institutional authority.”
A speech-act class expressing an attitude or psychological state about a situation.
Example: A speaker apologizes for arriving late.
Important distinction: Apologies and congratulations express attitudes; declarations require a different institutional relation.

questions.question: Which statement about Declaration is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: An authorized judge pronounces a sentence in court.
Institutional authority and procedures distinguish declarations from ordinary assertions about a legal outcome.
Anyone can successfully declare a defendant legally guilty in any casual conversation.
A speech act that changes an institutional state when successfully performed by an appropriate person.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Anyone can successfully declare a defendant legally guilty in any casual conversation.”
A speech act that changes an institutional state when successfully performed by an appropriate person.
Example: An authorized judge pronounces a sentence in court.
Important distinction: Institutional authority and procedures distinguish declarations from ordinary assertions about a legal outcome.

questions.question: Which statement about Presupposition is INACCURATE?
options: A presupposition must always be true in the actual world.
An illustration is: Sara stopped smoking normally presupposes that she used to smoke.
Background information presented as already taken for granted in an utterance.
Speakers can presuppose something false; hearers may challenge or accommodate it.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “A presupposition must always be true in the actual world.”
Background information presented as already taken for granted in an utterance.
Example: Sara stopped smoking normally presupposes that she used to smoke.
Important distinction: Speakers can presuppose something false; hearers may challenge or accommodate it.

questions.question: Which statement about Presupposition projection is INACCURATE?
options: Negating an utterance always removes every presupposition associated with it.
The tendency of some presuppositions to survive under negation or other operators.
An illustration is: Sara did not stop smoking commonly still suggests that Sara smoked before.
Projection is context-sensitive and differs across triggers; survival under negation is a useful diagnostic, not an exceptionless rule.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Negating an utterance always removes every presupposition associated with it.”
The tendency of some presuppositions to survive under negation or other operators.
Example: Sara did not stop smoking commonly still suggests that Sara smoked before.
Important distinction: Projection is context-sensitive and differs across triggers; survival under negation is a useful diagnostic, not an exceptionless rule.

questions.question: Which statement about Factive trigger is INACCURATE?
options: Compare believe: believing a proposition does not by itself make it factive.
An expression conventionally associated with presupposing the truth of its complement.
An illustration is: Sara regrets that she missed the bus normally takes the missed bus as background fact.
Regret normally presupposes that its complement is false.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Regret normally presupposes that its complement is false.”
An expression conventionally associated with presupposing the truth of its complement.
Example: Sara regrets that she missed the bus normally takes the missed bus as background fact.
Important distinction: Compare believe: believing a proposition does not by itself make it factive.

questions.question: Which statement about Person deixis is INACCURATE?
options: I always refers to the same named individual regardless of who is speaking.
An illustration is: I refers to the current speaker in an ordinary unquoted utterance.
Context-dependent reference anchored to participants in the speech event.
The conventional meaning identifies a participant role; context supplies the particular referent.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “I always refers to the same named individual regardless of who is speaking.”
Context-dependent reference anchored to participants in the speech event.
Example: I refers to the current speaker in an ordinary unquoted utterance.
Important distinction: The conventional meaning identifies a participant role; context supplies the particular referent.

questions.question: Which statement about Spatial deixis is INACCURATE?
options: Here has one unchanging geographical referent in every utterance.
Context-dependent reference to locations relative to a deictic anchor.
An illustration is: Put it here depends on the speaker's or another established spatial viewpoint.
The deictic centre can shift in narrative or reported discourse.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Here has one unchanging geographical referent in every utterance.”
Context-dependent reference to locations relative to a deictic anchor.
Example: Put it here depends on the speaker's or another established spatial viewpoint.
Important distinction: The deictic centre can shift in narrative or reported discourse.

questions.question: Which statement about Temporal deixis is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Tomorrow normally denotes the day after the day of speaking.
Tomorrow names the same calendar date in every conversation.
The anchor matters; quotation and narrative can change the relevant reference time.
Context-dependent reference to time relative to an utterance or other established anchor.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Tomorrow names the same calendar date in every conversation.”
Context-dependent reference to time relative to an utterance or other established anchor.
Example: Tomorrow normally denotes the day after the day of speaking.
Important distinction: The anchor matters; quotation and narrative can change the relevant reference time.

questions.question: Which statement about Social deixis is INACCURATE?
options: Social deixis is defined as the acoustic frequency of a vowel.
Honorifics and address choices can index status without literally describing physical distance.
Linguistic marking that indexes social relationships or status.
An illustration is: Choosing a respectful address form signals the relationship between participants.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Social deixis is defined as the acoustic frequency of a vowel.”
Linguistic marking that indexes social relationships or status.
Example: Choosing a respectful address form signals the relationship between participants.
Important distinction: Honorifics and address choices can index status without literally describing physical distance.

questions.question: Which statement about Discourse deixis is INACCURATE?
options: It differs from ordinary object reference, though the boundary with anaphora can require careful analysis.
Reference to a portion of discourse as discourse.
Discourse deixis must always refer to an object physically beside the speaker.
An illustration is: That was a strange thing to say uses that to point to a preceding utterance.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Discourse deixis must always refer to an object physically beside the speaker.”
Reference to a portion of discourse as discourse.
Example: That was a strange thing to say uses that to point to a preceding utterance.
Important distinction: It differs from ordinary object reference, though the boundary with anaphora can require careful analysis.

questions.question: Which statement about Anaphora is INACCURATE?
options: Pronouns may be anaphoric or deictic, so pronoun form alone does not establish the reference mechanism.
An illustration is: Sara found a key and put it in her bag uses it for the previously mentioned key.
Interpretation of an expression through an antecedent in discourse.
Every pronoun must point to something physically present and can never have a textual antecedent.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Every pronoun must point to something physically present and can never have a textual antecedent.”
Interpretation of an expression through an antecedent in discourse.
Example: Sara found a key and put it in her bag uses it for the previously mentioned key.
Important distinction: Pronouns may be anaphoric or deictic, so pronoun form alone does not establish the reference mechanism.

questions.question: Which statement about Accommodation is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: Hearing My sister is visiting, a listener provisionally accepts that the speaker has a sister.
Updating the shared assumptions to make an utterance's presupposition interpretable when appropriate.
Accommodation requires the hearer to accept every presupposition as unquestionably true.
A hearer may instead challenge an assumption; accommodation is a contextual interpretive move.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: “Accommodation requires the hearer to accept every presupposition as unquestionably true.”
Updating the shared assumptions to make an utterance's presupposition interpretable when appropriate.
Example: Hearing My sister is visiting, a listener provisionally accepts that the speaker has a sister.
Important distinction: A hearer may instead challenge an assumption; accommodation is a contextual interpretive move.

questions.question: A says Did all the students pass? B says Some did, perhaps all. Which conclusion is best?
options: B has contradicted the minimum existential claim.
Some logically entails not all in every ordinary use.
The not-all inference can be cancelled without semantic contradiction.
Quantity applies only to sound volume.
questions.explanation: Some conventionally asserts at least some; a not-all suggestion can arise as a scalar implicature. Perhaps all cancels that suggestion while retaining the explicit assertion.

questions.question: A warning makes a child step away from traffic. Which pairing is correct?
options: Warning: illocution; stepping away: perlocutionary effect.
questions.explanation: The warning is the act performed in saying something; the child's response is an effect on behaviour. The effect might fail even if the warning is appropriately performed.

questions.question: An unauthorized spectator says I sentence you to prison outside a court. What is the central issue?
options: The sentence has no recognizable words.
Every performative automatically changes legal status.
The institutional felicity conditions are not satisfied.
The utterance contains no finite verb.
questions.explanation: An institutional declaration requires appropriate authority and circumstances. A grammatically formed formula is insufficient to produce the legal result.

questions.question: During a storm, someone conspicuously says What perfect picnic weather! What is the likely Gricean analysis?
options: Overt flouting of quality supports an ironic interpretation.
A covert lie intended to establish the weather report as literally true.
A necessary entailment that no storm exists.
questions.explanation: The obvious mismatch can make literal truth implausible and invite an ironic interpretation. It differs from a concealed attempt to deceive about the actual weather.

questions.question: What is the safest interpretation of a two-line conversation lacking a clear situation?
options: There must be exactly one recoverable intention in all contexts.
Every ambiguous exchange is syntactically impossible.
Several pragmatic interpretations may remain possible.
questions.explanation: Pragmatic inference depends on context and assumptions. Without them, an analyst should not invent a single speaker intention and treat it as certain.

questions.question: A hearer responds Wait, you have a sister? to My sister is visiting. What has the hearer done?
options: Challenged or queried a presupposed background assumption.
Demonstrated that all pronouns are meaningless.
Confirmed that every presupposition is always shared.
questions.explanation: The possessive noun phrase commonly introduces a background assumption that the speaker has a sister. A hearer may question it instead of silently accommodating it.

concepts.definition: A conventional relationship between a linguistic form and its meaning, without a necessary natural resemblance.
concepts.example: English dog and Urdu kutta name the same kind of animal using different sound sequences.
concepts.false: Every word must physically resemble what it denotes.
concepts.note: Arbitrariness permits conventional variation across languages; it does not mean speakers choose meanings randomly during each conversation.

concepts.definition: The capacity to create and understand new messages by combining familiar linguistic resources.
concepts.example: A listener understands a new sentence about a purple robot teaching cricket on Mars.
concepts.false: A language contains only a fixed list of memorized complete messages.
concepts.note: Productivity concerns new combinations, not simply the number of words already stored.

concepts.definition: The capacity to communicate about entities or events beyond the immediate situation.
concepts.example: A speaker discusses a holiday planned for next year.
concepts.false: Language can refer only to objects visible at the moment of speaking.
concepts.note: References to the past, future, absent places and imaginary worlds illustrate displacement.

concepts.definition: Organization at two levels, where individually meaningless elements combine into meaningful units.
concepts.example: The sounds /k/, /æ/ and /t/ combine as cat, while another arrangement produces tack.
concepts.false: Every individual speech sound must have an independent lexical meaning.
concepts.note: Duality distinguishes the level of sound organization from the level of meaningful units.

concepts.definition: The organization of language into distinguishable units or categories.
concepts.example: Changing /p/ to /b/ distinguishes pat from bat rather than creating a continuous halfway word.
concepts.false: Linguistic categories are defined only by continuous changes in loudness.
concepts.note: Physical speech varies continuously, but linguistic analysis identifies categorical contrasts.

concepts.definition: Learning a particular language through exposure and interaction with its users.
concepts.example: A child raised with Urdu acquires Urdu rather than automatically acquiring the ancestral language of a distant family.
concepts.false: A child's particular language is determined solely by biological ancestry.
concepts.note: Biological capacities support acquisition, while experience determines which language or languages develop.

concepts.definition: The ability of participants to function as both producers and receivers of messages.
concepts.example: Two friends alternate between speaking and listening during a conversation.
concepts.false: One conversational participant can only send messages for life.
concepts.note: Interchangeability concerns communicative roles, not whether two words are synonyms.

concepts.definition: The ability to use language to discuss language itself.
concepts.example: A teacher explains that plural is a grammatical term.
concepts.false: Language cannot be used to describe its own forms.
concepts.note: This design property underlies metalinguistic explanation and grammatical discussion.

concepts.definition: A structured set of interacting patterns governing linguistic units.
concepts.example: English permits black cat but normally not cat black as an ordinary adjective-plus-noun expression.
concepts.false: Any order of familiar words is equally grammatical in a language.
concepts.note: Constraints depend on the language and construction; another language may permit a different order.

concepts.definition: A conventional pairing of a form with a meaning or concept.
concepts.example: The English form tree is associated with the concept of a woody plant.
concepts.false: A linguistic sign is identical to the physical object it refers to.
concepts.note: The sign and its referent differ: the word tree is not a tree.

concepts.definition: Using language primarily to communicate propositional information.
concepts.example: A notice states that the library closes at five.
concepts.false: Informative language cannot communicate facts about opening times.
concepts.note: A single utterance can have several functions; this label identifies its main informational purpose.

concepts.definition: Using language to negotiate relationships, attitudes and social roles.
concepts.example: A student addresses a lecturer as Professor to mark their relationship.
concepts.false: Forms of address never express social relationships.
concepts.note: Interpersonal meaning includes stance and relationship management, and may coexist with factual content.

concepts.definition: Using an appropriate utterance to carry out a socially recognized act.
concepts.example: An authorized official says I declare the meeting open in the proper setting.
concepts.false: Any speaker can legally marry any couple merely by saying a formula anywhere.
concepts.note: Authority, circumstances and accepted procedures matter for institutional performances.

concepts.definition: Using language to express feelings or emotional reactions.
concepts.example: A surprised spectator says Wow, what a finish!
concepts.false: Emotional expressions must always provide a neutral factual report.
concepts.note: Emotive language can express the speaker's state without successfully changing anyone else's emotion.

concepts.definition: Using language chiefly to establish or maintain social contact.
concepts.example: Two neighbours exchange Hello and Nice day while passing.
concepts.false: Every greeting primarily introduces new technical information.
concepts.note: Phatic exchanges help sustain relationships even when little new information is conveyed.

concepts.definition: Using language for enjoyment or verbal play.
concepts.example: Friends invent playful rhymes for amusement.
concepts.false: Language used for pleasure must always be a legal declaration.
concepts.note: Jokes, wordplay and playful verse may serve this function, often alongside other purposes.

concepts.definition: Using language to clarify a linguistic code or expression.
concepts.example: A learner asks What does morpheme mean?
concepts.false: Explaining a word's meaning cannot be a use of language.
concepts.note: Metalingual is a function label; reflexivity names the broader capacity making it possible.

concepts.definition: The vocal-auditory channel of linguistic communication.
concepts.example: A speaker produces an oral utterance that another person hears.
concepts.false: All human languages must use the vocal-auditory channel.
concepts.note: Speech is widespread, but natural signed languages use a visual-gestural modality.

concepts.definition: A natural linguistic system expressed through conventional visual-gestural forms.
concepts.example: Deaf signers combine signs according to the grammar of their community's sign language.
concepts.false: Natural signed languages lack grammar and merely mime spoken words.
concepts.note: Signed languages have productive grammars and are not universal across all communities.

concepts.definition: Conventional visible symbols used to represent aspects of language.
concepts.example: A learner records an Urdu sentence using the Urdu script.
concepts.false: A language cannot exist until it has a writing system.
concepts.note: Writing is historically later than speech and is not required for a community to have a full language.

concepts.definition: A speaker's internal knowledge of a linguistic system in a competence-performance distinction.
concepts.example: A speaker recognizes a grammatical sentence they have never heard before.
concepts.false: Competence consists only of flawless pronunciation in public speaking.
concepts.note: In this theoretical distinction, competence concerns knowledge rather than every detail of actual performance.

concepts.definition: Actual language use under real processing and situational conditions.
concepts.example: A tired speaker makes a slip despite knowing the intended construction.
concepts.false: Every hesitation proves that a speaker lacks grammatical knowledge.
concepts.note: Memory, attention and fatigue can affect performance without eliminating underlying knowledge.

concepts.definition: Investigating the patterns people use without treating social prestige as grammatical superiority.
concepts.example: A linguist records the systematic agreement patterns of a regional variety.
concepts.false: Only prestigious accents can have systematic linguistic rules.
concepts.note: Description can recognize social judgments while distinguishing them from structural analysis.

concepts.definition: The distinction between a linguistic system and the broader transmission of information.
concepts.example: Smoke from a fire communicates danger but does not by itself constitute a human language.
concepts.false: Every signal that conveys information is a full natural language.
concepts.note: Communication includes nonlinguistic signals; language is a particular structured capacity and social system.

concepts.definition: Using evidence and explicit analysis to investigate linguistic structure, use and acquisition.
concepts.example: A researcher tests a hypothesis about word order against recorded examples.
concepts.false: Linguistics consists entirely of listing etiquette rules for correct speech.
concepts.note: Linguistics includes many methods, but claims should be open to evidence and revision.

concepts.definition: The investigation of the physical production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
concepts.example: A researcher measures tongue position while someone produces [t].
concepts.false: Phonetics studies only the spelling of words.
concepts.note: Its articulatory, acoustic and auditory perspectives address different aspects of physical speech.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The investigation of sound patterns and contrasts in a linguistic system.
concepts.example: A researcher asks whether changing one sound changes a word's meaning in English.
concepts.false: Phonology is simply another name for the physics of sound waves.
concepts.note: Its questions include phonemes, allophones, phonotactics, stress and systematic alternations.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of the internal structure of words and the patterns forming them.
concepts.example: A researcher separates unhelpful into un-, help and -ful.
concepts.false: Morphology studies only the order of complete independent clauses.
concepts.note: It investigates meaningful or grammatical units inside words and relations among word forms.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of how words and phrases combine into larger grammatical structures.
concepts.example: An analyst compares The child opened the gate with an unacceptable reordering.
concepts.false: Syntax is the study of vocal-fold vibration.
concepts.note: Syntactic structures are hierarchical rather than merely unordered lists of words.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of conventional linguistic meaning, including word and sentence meaning.
concepts.example: An analyst explains why rose entails flower in an appropriate lexical sense.
concepts.false: Semantics examines only how loud a speaker sounds.
concepts.note: Context can help select a sense, but semantic analysis addresses encoded meaning and meaning relations.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of interpretation and action in context.
concepts.example: Can you open the window? is understood as a request during a hot lesson.
concepts.false: Pragmatics ignores who is speaking and the situation of an utterance.
concepts.note: It includes implicature, speech acts, deixis and contextual assumptions.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The theory and practice of compiling dictionaries.
concepts.example: An editor chooses definitions, examples and usage labels for dictionary entries.
concepts.false: Lexicography means diagnosing damage to language-related brain networks.
concepts.note: Dictionary making uses linguistic evidence, and modern practice often draws on corpora.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of vocabulary and the organization and relations of lexical items.
concepts.example: A scholar examines relations among words in a lexical field.
concepts.false: Lexicology is identical to physically printing a dictionary.
concepts.note: Lexicology investigates the lexicon, while lexicography concerns dictionary theory and practice.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of relationships between language and social life or social variation.
concepts.example: A researcher compares pronunciation across social groups and speaking styles.
concepts.false: Sociolinguistics treats age and social setting as irrelevant to language use.
concepts.note: Correlations require evidence and do not justify assuming that all members of a group speak alike.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of dialect variation, traditionally including its geographical distribution.
concepts.example: A map compares local words for the same object across districts.
concepts.false: Dialectology studies only changes in a single person's hearing.
concepts.note: Dialects may differ in pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar; accent refers principally to pronunciation.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of mental processes involved in language acquisition, comprehension and production.
concepts.example: An experiment measures how quickly listeners recognize a spoken word.
concepts.false: Psycholinguistics concerns only the legal wording of contracts.
concepts.note: Acquisition and disorders are relevant topics, but the field also studies ordinary processing.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of neural mechanisms supporting language.
concepts.example: A researcher relates language performance after a brain lesion to neural damage.
concepts.false: Neurolinguistics assumes every language ability lies in one isolated brain point.
concepts.note: Language depends on interacting networks; lesion and imaging evidence require careful interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The investigation of language organization and meaning across stretches of interaction or text.
concepts.example: An analyst studies how turns connect during an interview.
concepts.false: Discourse analysis must ignore relationships between successive utterances.
concepts.note: Its units may exceed a single sentence and include interactional organization and textual interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: Linguistic investigation of choices and patterns associated with effects in texts or speech.
concepts.example: A critic examines how repeated short clauses create urgency in a passage.
concepts.false: Stylistics judges a text without examining any linguistic features.
concepts.note: It connects patterns to interpretations with textual evidence rather than impression alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: Linguistic analysis of literature and its interpretive effects.
concepts.example: A researcher studies foregrounded repetition in a poem.
concepts.false: Literary stylistics excludes syntax and sound from analysis.
concepts.note: It may draw on phonetics, grammar, semantics, pragmatics and discourse analysis.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The investigation of real-world problems involving language.
concepts.example: A team evaluates language teaching materials for multilingual learners.
concepts.false: Applied linguistics is limited to correcting punctuation.
concepts.note: Teaching is important, but translation, assessment, policy and other practical problems also fall within its scope.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The computational modelling and processing of natural language.
concepts.example: A system is developed to parse Urdu sentences automatically.
concepts.false: Computational linguistics studies Java syntax instead of human language.
concepts.note: Programming is a tool; natural-language structure and processing are central objects of inquiry.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: Approaches relating language to general cognition, conceptualization and experience.
concepts.example: An analyst investigates the conceptual metaphor TIME IS MONEY.
concepts.false: Cognitive linguistics defines language as unrelated to human conceptualization.
concepts.note: It is an approach or family of approaches, not simply the name for all laboratory language experiments.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of language in relation to culture and human social practices.
concepts.example: An ethnographer examines how kinship terms organize social relationships.
concepts.false: Anthropological linguistics investigates only isolated sound waves in a laboratory.
concepts.note: Linguistic anthropology and anthropological linguistics overlap, though institutional emphases differ.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The investigation of language change and historical relationships among languages.
concepts.example: A scholar reconstructs earlier forms using systematic correspondences across related languages.
concepts.false: Any two words that sound alike prove that their languages are related.
concepts.note: Genetic relationships require systematic evidence, not isolated resemblance or borrowing alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The comparison and classification of languages by structural properties.
concepts.example: A study compares SOV and SVO word-order patterns across unrelated languages.
concepts.false: Typology groups languages only by their writing systems.
