concepts.note: Structural similarity does not by itself establish descent from a common ancestor.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The systematic study of language using organized collections of authentic language data.
concepts.example: A researcher searches a tagged corpus to compare frequent verb-noun combinations.
concepts.false: Corpus linguistics consists only of collecting files without analyzing them.
concepts.note: Corpus design, sampling, annotation and interpretation affect what conclusions are justified.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: Linguistic investigation of language in legal and investigative contexts.
concepts.example: An expert examines how the wording of a police interview affects interpretation.
concepts.false: Forensic linguistics guarantees identification of an author from any short sentence.
concepts.note: Its findings are evidence-based and probabilistic where appropriate, not infallible identification.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of learning additional languages beyond initial language acquisition.
concepts.example: A researcher tracks how adult Urdu speakers develop English tense marking.
concepts.false: Second-language acquisition means only compiling bilingual dictionaries.
concepts.note: It examines learning processes and outcomes; it does not imply that only a second language can be studied.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: A broad teaching label for investigation of language's internal structural systems.
concepts.example: A course groups phonology, morphology and syntax as core internal analyses.
concepts.false: Every textbook must draw exactly the same boundary around microlinguistics.
concepts.note: Micro/macro boundaries vary, especially for pragmatics, and are not universal divisions of nature.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: The study of how speech organs produce speech sounds.
concepts.example: An investigator tracks lip closure while a person says [p].
concepts.false: Articulatory phonetics measures only dictionary word frequency.
concepts.note: Articulators include the tongue and lips; the larynx and airflow also matter for production.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The study of measurable physical properties of speech signals.
concepts.example: An investigator measures frequency and duration from a recorded vowel.
concepts.false: Acoustic phonetics classifies sounds solely by their written letters.
concepts.note: Frequency, amplitude, duration and spectral structure are acoustic properties.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The study of hearing and perception of speech sounds.
concepts.example: Listeners judge whether two recorded consonants sound different.
concepts.false: Auditory phonetics concerns only the motion of the tongue.
concepts.note: The auditory system receives acoustic signals, while perception also involves interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Speech airflow powered by air moving out from the lungs.
concepts.example: A person produces an ordinary English [s] while exhaling.
concepts.false: Ordinary English speech is primarily produced by air flowing into the lungs.
concepts.note: Most English speech sounds use this mechanism, although other languages also use nonpulmonic consonants.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Vocal-fold vibration during the production of a sound.
concepts.example: The folds vibrate during a sustained [z].
concepts.false: Voicing is defined as making a sound louder than a whisper.
concepts.note: Compare [z] and [s]: the key contrast is laryngeal vibration rather than loudness.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation involving both lips.
concepts.example: Both lips come together to produce [p], [b] or [m].
concepts.false: Bilabial articulation requires the tongue tip against the upper teeth.
concepts.note: Place identifies the articulators; manner distinguishes a stop such as [p] from a nasal such as [m].
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation involving the lower lip and upper teeth.
concepts.example: The lower lip approaches the upper teeth for [f].
concepts.false: [f] is formed by complete closure of both lips.
concepts.note: English [f] and [v] share place and manner but differ in voicing.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation involving the tongue and the teeth.
concepts.example: English [θ] in thin is produced at the teeth.
concepts.false: English [θ] is a bilabial nasal.
concepts.note: Some descriptions call these English sounds interdental; [ð] is the voiced counterpart.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation at or near the ridge behind the upper teeth.
concepts.example: The tongue contacts the alveolar ridge during [t].
concepts.false: Alveolar sounds require closure of the vocal folds as their oral place.
concepts.note: English [t], [d], [n], [s], [z] and [l] are commonly classified as alveolar.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation involving the tongue dorsum and soft palate.
concepts.example: The back of the tongue makes closure for [k].
concepts.false: Velar articulation is made with the upper teeth and lower lip.
concepts.note: [k], [ɡ] and [ŋ] share a velar place, though they differ in other properties.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation whose relevant constriction is at the glottis.
concepts.example: The vocal folds close to produce a glottal stop [ʔ].
concepts.false: A glottal stop requires the lips to seal the mouth.
concepts.note: Glottal describes place in the larynx; it is not a synonym for a velar constriction.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A manner involving complete closure followed by release or another transition.
concepts.example: Air is briefly blocked in the mouth during [p].
concepts.false: Stops require continuous narrow-channel friction throughout their articulation.
concepts.note: Oral stops contrast with fricatives; not every stop has a strong audible release in every context.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A manner involving turbulent airflow through a narrow constriction.
concepts.example: A sustained [s] produces audible friction.
concepts.false: A fricative always involves an oral closure that blocks airflow completely.
concepts.note: Fricatives can differ in place and voicing, as in [f], [s] and [z].
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A stop closure followed by a closely coordinated fricative release.
concepts.example: English [tʃ] in church begins with closure and releases into friction.
concepts.false: Every affricate is simply a vowel followed by a nasal.
concepts.note: Affricates often function as single consonant units despite their complex articulation.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Production with an open nasal passage so air escapes through the nose.
concepts.example: The velum is lowered during [m].
concepts.false: Nasal consonants require the nasal passage to be completely sealed.
concepts.note: A nasal consonant typically has oral closure alongside nasal airflow.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation with a constriction that normally does not produce fricative turbulence.
concepts.example: The tongue approaches the palate for [j] in yes.
concepts.false: Every approximant has the same complete closure as [p].
concepts.note: Glides and liquids are often grouped as approximants, with finer distinctions in their airflow.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The dimension associated with the tongue body's relative high or low position in vowel production.
concepts.example: [i] has a higher tongue position than [a].
concepts.false: Vowel height is the same as a speaker's habitual loudness.
concepts.note: High/close and low/open are alternative descriptive labels in vowel classification.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The dimension associated with the tongue body's relative front or back position.
concepts.example: [i] is front while [u] is back.
concepts.false: Backness means how far a written vowel appears from the end of a word.
concepts.note: Height, backness and lip rounding jointly help describe vowel quality.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The protrusion or rounding of the lips during speech.
concepts.example: A typical [u] is produced with rounded lips.
concepts.false: All vowels in all languages must be rounded.
concepts.note: Rounding is distinct from backness: front rounded vowels occur in many languages.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A vowel with a noticeable quality change within one syllable.
concepts.example: The vowel of many English pronunciations of my glides as [aɪ].
concepts.false: A diphthong must consist of two separate syllables.
concepts.note: Accent matters: vowel realizations and phonemic analyses differ across English varieties.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The mid central vowel represented by [ə], often occurring in unstressed syllables in English.
concepts.example: Many English speakers use [ə] in the first syllable of about.
concepts.false: Schwa is the IPA symbol for a voiceless bilabial stop.
concepts.note: Schwa's distribution varies by language and accent; it is not inherently unstressed in every language.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A speech sound considered as a physical phonetic realization.
concepts.example: An analyst transcribes an actual aspirated release as [pʰ].
concepts.false: A phone is a written letter of an alphabet.
concepts.note: Square brackets conventionally mark phonetic transcription.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A contrastive unit in a language's sound system.
concepts.example: Substituting /b/ for /p/ changes pat to bat in English.
concepts.false: Two sounds belong to different phonemes whenever their waveforms differ at all.
concepts.note: Contrast is language-specific; a phoneme is an abstract category rather than a single identical waveform.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A contextually or otherwise conditioned realization of a phoneme that does not by itself create a lexical contrast in that system.
concepts.example: English /p/ is aspirated in pin but typically unaspirated after /s/ in spin.
concepts.false: English [pʰ] and [p] must distinguish words in every position.
concepts.note: The same phonetic distinction can be allophonic in one language and phonemic in another.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Two words differing in one sound in the same position with a difference in meaning.
concepts.example: English sip and zip differ only in their initial consonants.
concepts.false: Two words form a minimal pair whenever they rhyme, regardless of other differences.
concepts.note: Minimal pairs provide strong evidence for phonemic contrast in the language being analyzed.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A pattern in which two sounds occur in mutually exclusive environments.
concepts.example: Aspirated and unaspirated English voiceless stops follow predictable environments in a simplified analysis.
concepts.false: Complementary distribution means the sounds occur in exactly the same environments.
concepts.note: Distribution supports an allophonic analysis when phonetic similarity and other evidence also fit.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A transcription emphasizing contrastive categories while omitting much phonetic detail.
concepts.example: An English word is written with /p/ without marking aspiration.
concepts.false: Broad transcription must record every small articulatory detail.
concepts.note: Slashes commonly mark phonemic transcription; narrow phonetic detail is usually bracketed.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A transcription including comparatively detailed phonetic properties.
concepts.example: An analyst writes [pʰ] to mark aspiration explicitly.
concepts.false: Narrow transcription is defined by the use of ordinary spelling alone.
concepts.note: Diacritics can mark aspiration, nasalization and other details relevant to an analysis.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A display showing how a signal's spectral energy varies over time.
concepts.example: Time runs horizontally and frequency vertically, with shading representing energy.
concepts.false: The vertical axis of a conventional spectrogram represents grammatical tense.
concepts.note: Display settings affect appearance, so darkness is not a universal ranking of all vowels above all consonants.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Resonant frequency regions of the vocal tract reflected in the speech spectrum.
concepts.example: An analyst compares F1 and F2 to investigate vowel quality.
concepts.false: Formants are identical to the repetition rate of vocal-fold vibration.
concepts.note: Fundamental frequency concerns periodicity; formants concern resonances shaped by the vocal tract.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The repetition rate of a periodic waveform, related in voiced speech to vocal-fold vibration.
concepts.example: A voiced segment has a fundamental frequency measured in hertz.
concepts.false: Fundamental frequency is measured in seconds and means segment duration.
concepts.note: Perceived pitch is related to fundamental frequency, but physical and perceptual measures are not identical.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Relative prominence assigned to syllables within words or larger structures.
concepts.example: The first syllable is prominent in the English noun REcord.
concepts.false: Stress is determined entirely by which letters are capitalized in normal spelling.
concepts.note: Duration, pitch and intensity can contribute to stress, with language-specific patterns.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Patterns of pitch variation over phrases or utterances.
concepts.example: A speaker changes a sentence's pitch contour to convey a particular interactional stance.
concepts.false: Every question in every language must have rising intonation.
concepts.note: Contour interpretation depends on construction, language, variety and context.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A process in which one sound becomes more similar to a nearby sound.
concepts.example: In casual speech, an alveolar nasal may become bilabial before a bilabial consonant.
concepts.false: Assimilation means a sound must become less like its neighbour.
concepts.note: Coarticulatory pressures often motivate assimilation, but the precise patterns are language-specific.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Constraints on permissible sound sequences and syllable patterns in a language.
concepts.example: English allows /str/ at the start of street but not every imaginable initial cluster.
concepts.false: A cluster impossible in English must be impossible in every language.
concepts.note: Phonotactic restrictions differ across languages and concern patterns beyond individual sound inventories.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The smallest unit with a meaning or grammatical function in a morphological analysis.
concepts.example: Cats contains cat and a plural marker.
concepts.false: Every morpheme must be an entire written word.
concepts.note: A morpheme may be free or bound; grammatical meaning counts even without a concrete object referent.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: An observable form realizing a morpheme.
concepts.example: The sound [s] realizes the plural morpheme in cats.
concepts.false: A morph is an abstract meaning with no realization.
concepts.note: Morpheme names the analytical unit; morph identifies its realization in a particular form.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: An alternative realization of the same morpheme.
concepts.example: English regular plurals have [s], [z] and [ɪz] realizations.
concepts.false: Alternative plural allomorphs must express different grammatical numbers.
concepts.note: Allomorphs preserve the relevant grammatical contribution despite differences in form.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A morpheme capable of occurring as a word on its own.
concepts.example: Book can occur alone and also inside books.
concepts.false: A free morpheme must always attach to another morpheme.
concepts.note: A complex word such as duster is not a single free morpheme merely because it can stand alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A morpheme that cannot ordinarily occur independently as a word.
concepts.example: The past-tense suffix -ed attaches to a verbal base.
concepts.false: Every bound morpheme is a complete independent sentence.
concepts.note: Affixes are bound, but bound roots also occur, so bound morpheme and affix are not exact synonyms.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A morpheme contributing substantial content meaning.
concepts.example: The root tiger contributes the animal concept in tigers.
concepts.false: Lexical morphemes are restricted to articles and conjunctions.
concepts.note: Lexical roots often belong to open classes such as nouns, verbs and adjectives.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A morpheme contributing grammatical organization or relational information.
concepts.example: The article the marks a noun phrase as definite in a suitable context.
concepts.false: Functional morphemes have no grammatical contribution at all.
concepts.note: The category includes free function words and, in broader usage, bound grammatical markers.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Morphology forming a new lexeme or a new lexical meaning, sometimes changing word class.
concepts.example: Adding un- to happy creates unhappy.
concepts.false: Derivation must always change the grammatical category of its base.
concepts.note: Unhappy remains an adjective; category preservation does not prevent an operation from being derivational.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Morphology expressing grammatical contrasts within a lexeme's paradigm.
concepts.example: Walk and walked express different grammatical forms of the same verb.
concepts.false: English past-tense inflection always creates a new noun lexeme.
concepts.note: Inflection generally preserves lexical category and core lexical identity.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: An affix attached before its base.
concepts.example: Re- precedes write in rewrite.
concepts.false: A prefix must occur after the root.
concepts.note: Position defines a prefix; whether it is derivational or inflectional depends on its function in the language.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: An affix attached after its base.
concepts.example: -ness follows kind in kindness.
concepts.false: A suffix must be inserted in the middle of a root.
concepts.note: English suffixes can be derivational or inflectional, as -ness and plural -s illustrate.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: An affix inserted within a root or base.
concepts.example: Tagalog sulat and sumulat illustrate an inserted -um-.
concepts.false: The English plural men is formed by inserting an ordinary infix into man.
concepts.note: Men illustrates internal vowel change; genuine infixation requires an inserted morphological element.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: The basic lexical core remaining after relevant affixes are removed.
concepts.example: Help is the root in unhelpfulness.
concepts.false: A root is always the final inflectional ending of a word.
concepts.note: Roots can be free or bound; not every root can occur as an independent word.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A form to which a morphological operation applies.
concepts.example: Helpful is the base to which un- attaches in unhelpful.
concepts.false: A base must contain exactly one morpheme.
concepts.note: A base may be a root or an already complex form.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A form to which an inflectional operation applies in a common introductory usage.
concepts.example: Worker is the stem receiving plural -s in workers.
concepts.false: A stem can never contain a derivational suffix.
concepts.note: Stem and base terminology varies somewhat across frameworks; the intended definition should be stated.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English plural ending.
concepts.example: Dogs ends in [z], cats in [s], and buses in [ɪz] in many descriptions.
concepts.false: The plural ending in dogs is normally the same voiceless [s] as in cats.
concepts.note: A sibilant requires the syllabic variant; otherwise the preceding segment's voicing normally conditions the ending.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Phonologically conditioned realization of the regular English past-tense ending.
concepts.example: Walked has [t], played [d], and wanted [ɪd] in common transcriptions.
concepts.false: Every written -ed ending necessarily forms a separate syllable.
concepts.note: The syllabic variant follows /t/ or /d/; other environments condition [t] or [d].
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A morphological relation involving forms with substantially different roots.
concepts.example: Go and went are related as present and past forms of one verb.
concepts.false: Suppletion is merely adding regular -ed to every verb.
concepts.note: The relation is grammatical despite the absence of an ordinary predictable shared root shape.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A plural form without an overt plural affix in an appropriate analysis.
concepts.example: One sheep and three sheep share the same overt noun form.
concepts.false: A noun without a visible suffix can never be plural.
concepts.note: Number can be identified from syntax and context even when the noun has no overt plural marker.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A morphological pattern realized by changing a vowel inside a base.
concepts.example: Sing, sang and sung differ in their internal vowels.
concepts.false: Internal vowel change requires a detachable infix in every case.
concepts.note: Internal modification differs from concatenating a separate prefix or suffix.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Formation of a word from two or more lexical bases.
concepts.example: Toothbrush combines tooth and brush.
concepts.false: A compound must be written as one uninterrupted string in every case.
concepts.note: Spacing and hyphenation do not reliably determine compound status on their own.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A change in lexical category without an overt derivational affix.
concepts.example: The noun bottle is used as a verb in They bottle the juice.
concepts.false: Conversion always requires the suffix -ness.
concepts.note: Also called zero derivation in some accounts, this process requires attention to actual use and analysis.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: The number of meaningful or grammatical units identified in a word.
concepts.example: Unhelpful contains three units: un-, help and -ful.
concepts.false: The number of morphemes must equal the number of syllables.
concepts.note: Teacher has two morphemes, while some multisyllabic words such as banana are monomorphemic.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A common English ordering in which derivation is nearer the root than outer inflection.
concepts.example: Workers has work + -er + plural -s.
concepts.false: Workers is normally built by adding agentive -er outside already plural works.
concepts.note: Morphological hierarchy matters; this English tendency should not be universalized without qualification.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A phrase headed by a noun or nominal element in a traditional introductory analysis.
concepts.example: The very old house functions as subject in The very old house collapsed.
concepts.false: A noun phrase must always contain at least two written words.
concepts.note: A single noun or pronoun can form a phrase; determiner-phrase analyses provide a different theoretical treatment.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A phrase headed by a preposition, often with a complement.
concepts.example: Under the table contains the preposition under and its complement.
concepts.false: A phrase headed by under becomes an adjective phrase merely because it modifies a noun.
concepts.note: Phrase category follows the head; grammatical function and phrase category must be distinguished.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A phrase headed by an adjective.
concepts.example: Very proud of her work is headed by proud.
concepts.false: Nice blue shirt is an adjective phrase headed by shirt.
concepts.note: Nice blue shirt is a noun phrase; adjective modifiers do not change its nominal head.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A phrase headed by an adverb.
concepts.example: Quite slowly is headed by slowly.
concepts.false: In a loud voice is an adverb phrase by head category.
concepts.note: In a loud voice is a prepositional phrase that may function as an adverbial.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A phrase headed by a verb, with its dependents according to the framework used.
concepts.example: Has eaten the apple includes a verbal head and its object in a common syntactic analysis.
concepts.false: Every account limits a verb phrase to auxiliaries and excludes objects.
concepts.note: Some school grammars use a narrower verb-group label; state the adopted framework when boundaries matter.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A nonfinite construction based on an infinitive verb.
concepts.example: To read novels functions as the complement of likes in She likes to read novels.
concepts.false: Infinitival to always functions as a preposition taking a noun object.
concepts.note: Many modern grammars treat such units as nonfinite clauses rather than simply infinitive phrases.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A nonfinite -ing construction traditionally associated with a nominal function.
concepts.example: Reading novels is relaxing places reading novels in subject position.
concepts.false: Every word ending in -ing is a gerund functioning as a noun.
concepts.note: Compare a progressive verb in is reading; modern analyses often use a unified gerund-participial category.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A participial construction modifying a nominal expression or supplying supplementary information.
concepts.example: The child wearing a red hat waved uses wearing a red hat to modify child.
concepts.false: Every participial modifier must be enclosed in commas.
concepts.note: Restrictive modifiers often lack commas; supplementary participial constructions are commonly set off.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A supplementary construction with its own subject-like element, often without a finite verb.
concepts.example: Her eyes on the clock, Sara waited for the bus.
concepts.false: An absolute construction must always contain a finite past-tense verb.
concepts.note: The construction comments on the accompanying situation; her eyes and on the clock form its internal relation.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A clause capable of functioning as a complete sentence in ordinary use.
concepts.example: Tara ate a cheese roll can stand independently.
concepts.false: Every clause introduced by although is independent.
concepts.note: Independence concerns syntactic status, not whether a reader needs any wider context to understand a reference.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A clause syntactically subordinate to another construction.
concepts.example: After she watched the news is subordinate in Tara ate after she watched the news.
concepts.false: A dependent clause must lack a verb.
concepts.note: Finite subordinate clauses often have an overt subject and verb, while nonfinite clauses may omit an overt subject.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Internalized linguistic knowledge supporting a speaker's patterns and judgments.
concepts.example: A child uses word-order patterns without being able to state a school grammar rule.
concepts.false: Mental grammar exists only after a child has completed a grammar textbook.
concepts.note: Implicit knowledge is distinct from conscious terminology and explicit classroom instruction.

concepts.definition: An account of the patterns actually found in a language or variety.
concepts.example: A grammar records a community's consistent use of multiple negation.
concepts.false: A descriptive grammar must condemn every nonstandard construction as structureless.
concepts.note: A nonstandard pattern can be systematic even when institutions discourage it.

concepts.definition: Norms recommending which forms people should use in particular contexts.
concepts.example: A style manual recommends a particular form for formal examination writing.
concepts.false: Prescriptive advice is automatically a complete account of all native-speaker usage.
concepts.note: Prescriptions may be useful for a register, but they differ from a description of every variety.

concepts.definition: A grammar organized to support language teaching and learning.
concepts.example: A textbook explains English question formation with practice exercises.
concepts.false: A pedagogical grammar must assume learners already know every language rule explicitly.
concepts.note: It may simplify or sequence material, and need not compare the target language with a first language in every lesson.

concepts.definition: A theoretical proposal about innate constraints or capacities specific to human language in generative approaches.
concepts.example: A generative account asks which aspects of possible grammars are biologically constrained.
concepts.false: Universal Grammar is a proven list of identical surface sentences in all languages.
concepts.note: The hypothesis and its scope are debated; it is not identical to any observed cross-linguistic generalization.

concepts.definition: Conformity to the structural patterns of a specified language variety in an analysis.
concepts.example: The children are playing conforms to standard English agreement.
concepts.false: A sentence becomes ungrammatical merely because it describes an imaginary event.
concepts.note: Grammaticality differs from truth, plausibility, politeness and stylistic preference.

concepts.definition: Speakers' judgments of how natural or usable an expression seems in context.
concepts.example: A highly nested sentence feels difficult despite following a proposed rule system.
concepts.false: Acceptability is unaffected by memory, context or processing demands.
concepts.note: Acceptability can reflect grammatical knowledge together with processing and contextual factors.

concepts.definition: A theoretical separation of linguistic knowledge from its actual use.
concepts.example: A speaker knows a construction but produces a tired slip while saying it.
concepts.false: A single speech error necessarily describes the full grammar of a community.
concepts.note: Performance data are evidence for competence, but interpretation must consider processing conditions.

concepts.definition: The inventory of lexical knowledge, including information about words and morphemes.
concepts.example: A speaker knows that give typically permits a recipient and a theme.
concepts.false: The mental lexicon contains only spelling and never grammatical information.
concepts.note: Pronunciation, meaning and combinatorial properties may be part of lexical knowledge.

concepts.definition: The sound-related interface representation in generative models using the PF label.
concepts.example: A derivation is interpreted on its pronunciation side at PF in a simplified model.
concepts.false: PF is the abbreviation for pragmatic function in the lecture's generative model.
concepts.note: PF is a theoretical representation, not simply the visible written form of a sentence.

concepts.definition: A meaning-related interface representation in generative models using the LF label.
concepts.example: A model uses LF to represent aspects of interpretation such as scope.
concepts.false: LF means the physical waveform recorded by a microphone.
concepts.note: PF/LF terminology belongs to particular frameworks and should not be presented as a complete theory-neutral description.

concepts.definition: Development of a linguistic system through experience and learning.
concepts.example: A child develops productive word combinations through interaction.
concepts.false: Every child follows an identical timetable and produces the same first words.
concepts.note: Broad developmental patterns coexist with substantial individual, linguistic and environmental variation.

concepts.definition: Application of a productive pattern to a form that is irregular in adult usage.
concepts.example: A child says goed where the adult form is went.
concepts.false: A child's use of goed shows only exact imitation of adult went.
concepts.note: The error provides evidence for pattern generalization alongside learning of exceptional forms.

concepts.definition: Knowledge expressed in skilled use without necessarily being consciously verbalized.
concepts.example: A fluent speaker chooses a natural word order but cannot explain the rule.
concepts.false: Implicit linguistic knowledge requires memorizing the name of every grammatical category.
concepts.note: Explicit rule knowledge and fluent implicit performance can dissociate.

concepts.definition: Consciously accessible knowledge that can be stated or reflected on.
concepts.example: A learner recites the rule for forming a regular English plural.
concepts.false: Being able to recite a rule always guarantees effortless real-time use.
concepts.note: Explicit knowledge can support learning but does not automatically equal fluent performance.

concepts.definition: The linguistic principle that natural dialects are systematic rather than inherently deficient.
concepts.example: A linguist treats regional agreement patterns as rule-governed.
concepts.false: Socially prestigious dialects are inherently more logical in all grammatical respects.
concepts.note: Social opportunities associated with standard varieties are real, but do not establish structural superiority.

concepts.definition: A socially established variety used in education, administration or other institutional settings.
concepts.example: A school adopts standard written English for examination essays.
concepts.false: A standard variety is the only variety with a grammar.
concepts.note: Standardization is social and historical; other varieties also have structured linguistic systems.

concepts.definition: The linguistic patterns associated with an individual speaker.
concepts.example: One speaker consistently prefers a particular pronunciation and expression.
concepts.false: An idiolect is necessarily a separate national language.
concepts.note: Individual patterns interact with community varieties and change across context and time.

concepts.definition: Investigation of a linguistic system at a particular time or period.
concepts.example: A study describes present-day Urdu case marking without tracing its history.
concepts.false: Synchronic analysis must reconstruct several ancestral stages.
concepts.note: A synchronic description can involve variation; it does not mean every speaker uses identical forms.

concepts.definition: Investigation of linguistic change through time.
concepts.example: A study traces the loss of certain English inflectional endings across centuries.
concepts.false: Diachronic analysis examines only the current acoustic pitch of a single vowel token.
concepts.note: It concerns historical development, which differs from description at a single period.

concepts.definition: A proposed property or tendency holding across languages, stated with an appropriate scope.
concepts.example: A typologist tests whether a structural pattern occurs across a diverse language sample.
concepts.false: A pattern observed in two related languages is automatically a universal.
concepts.note: Absolute claims and statistical tendencies require different evidence and should not be conflated.

concepts.definition: Comparison of structural patterns across languages.
concepts.example: Languages are compared according to their dominant ordering of subject, object and verb.
concepts.false: Two languages with SOV order must belong to the same historical family.
concepts.note: Typological grouping and genetic classification answer different questions.

concepts.definition: Observations drawn from systematically collected language data.
concepts.example: Repeated corpus examples support the claim that a collocation is frequent in a register.
concepts.false: A construction absent from one small corpus is necessarily impossible in the language.
concepts.note: Sampling and corpus size limit what absence and frequency can show.

concepts.definition: Collection of linguistic evidence through targeted tasks or questions to speakers.
concepts.example: A researcher asks speakers to judge alternative sentences in a controlled context.
concepts.false: Elicited judgments never depend on task design or the context supplied.
concepts.note: Elicitation complements naturally occurring data and benefits from multiple speakers and careful controls.

concepts.definition: Complementary analytical perspectives on different aspects of linguistic organization.
concepts.example: One sentence is examined for sound patterns, word structure, syntax and meaning.
concepts.false: Explaining a sentence's syntax automatically replaces every semantic and pragmatic analysis.
concepts.note: Levels interact but address distinguishable questions; lists of levels vary across teaching frameworks.

concepts.definition: A word or group of words functioning as a structural unit within a larger expression.
concepts.example: The old house can be replaced by it in The old house collapsed.
concepts.false: Any arbitrary consecutive sequence of words must form a constituent.
concepts.note: Constituency concerns hierarchical units; substitution, movement and coordination can provide evidence.

concepts.definition: The units into which a larger structure is divided at its next structural level.
concepts.example: In a simple analysis, The child and laughed are the immediate constituents of The child laughed.
concepts.false: Immediate constituents must always be individual letters.
concepts.note: Immediate units differ from the smallest terminal units reached after further analysis.

concepts.definition: The smallest units represented at the leaves of a particular syntactic analysis.
concepts.example: Individual words appear as leaves in a word-level tree of a sentence.
concepts.false: The terminal units of every possible grammatical analysis must be whole sentences.
concepts.note: The chosen level matters; analyses incorporating morphology may decompose words further.

concepts.definition: Organization in which smaller units combine into nested larger units.
concepts.example: The noun phrase the child with a hat contains the smaller prepositional phrase with a hat.
concepts.false: Syntactic structure is fully captured by listing words alphabetically.
concepts.note: Hierarchy explains relations that linear order alone cannot capture.

concepts.definition: The central element that determines important properties of a phrase.
concepts.example: Proud heads the adjective phrase very proud of her work.
concepts.false: The first written word in every phrase is necessarily its head.
concepts.note: The head's position varies across constructions and languages.

concepts.definition: A grammatical relation associated with properties such as agreement and clause structure.
concepts.example: In The window was broken by Ali, the window is the subject.
concepts.false: The subject must always intentionally perform an action.
concepts.note: Grammatical subject and semantic agent differ, especially in passives and experiencer constructions.

concepts.definition: A verb-dependent nominal grammatical relation in a transitive construction.
concepts.example: The book is the direct object in Sara read the book.
concepts.false: Every phrase after a verb is a direct object.
concepts.note: A prepositional phrase such as to school is not a direct object merely because it follows a verb.

concepts.definition: An expression predicating a property or identity of the subject after a linking verb.
concepts.example: A doctor is the subject complement in Amina is a doctor.
concepts.false: The C in SVC stands for consonant.
concepts.note: Subject complements differ from objects: they characterize or identify the subject.

concepts.definition: An expression predicating a property or identity of an object.
concepts.example: Happy describes the object him in The news made him happy.
concepts.false: An object complement must identify the grammatical subject instead of the object.
concepts.note: The pattern is often labelled SVOC, with an object plus a predication about it.

concepts.definition: A modifier not selected as a required complement in the relevant construction.
concepts.example: Yesterday adds optional time information in Sara smiled yesterday.
concepts.false: Every optional modifier is automatically the verb's direct object.
concepts.note: Optionality is a useful clue but is not a complete universal test of adjunct status.

concepts.definition: A clause pattern consisting of a subject and an intransitive verb.
concepts.example: The baby slept is a basic SV clause.
concepts.false: An SV pattern requires an overt direct object.
concepts.note: Additional optional modifiers may occur without making the verb transitive.

concepts.definition: A clause pattern with a subject, transitive verb and direct object.
concepts.example: Sara opened the door has Sara, opened and the door as S, V and O.
concepts.false: She goes to school is an SVO example because school occurs after the verb.
concepts.note: In goes to school, to school is a prepositional phrase; in traditional clause-pattern accounts it is an adverbial.

concepts.definition: A clause pattern with a subject, linking verb and subject complement.
concepts.example: Ali is tired has tired as the subject complement.
concepts.false: The final element of SVC is always a consonant sound.
concepts.note: Linking verbs connect a subject with an identifying or descriptive complement.

concepts.definition: A clause pattern containing a subject, verb and adverbial, often a required adverbial in strict pattern analyses.
concepts.example: She lives in Lahore uses a location adverbial in a traditional SVA analysis.
concepts.false: The A in SVA means that only a single-word adverb can appear there.
concepts.note: Adverbial is a function that can be realized by a prepositional phrase or another construction.

concepts.definition: A clause pattern with subject, verb, indirect object and direct object.
concepts.example: Sara gave Ali a book has Ali as indirect object and a book as direct object.
concepts.false: SVOO requires two independent clauses.
concepts.note: The two objects occupy different grammatical relations; prepositional alternatives may express similar participant relations.

concepts.definition: A clause pattern with subject, verb, object and object complement.
concepts.example: They painted the door green contains an object and a property predicated of it.
concepts.false: Green is a second independent clause in They painted the door green.
concepts.note: Contrast a book in gave Ali a book: it is an object, not a property predicated of Ali.

concepts.definition: A clause pattern with subject, verb, object and an adverbial required by the construction.
concepts.example: Sara put the book on the shelf contains a required location after the object.
concepts.false: Put the book normally supplies the full intended placement construction without a location.
concepts.note: Required complements and optional adjuncts must be distinguished when assigning strict clause patterns.

concepts.definition: A clause form conventionally associated with making a statement.
concepts.example: The train is late has ordinary declarative form.
concepts.false: A declarative form can never be used to make a request indirectly.
concepts.note: Clause form and speech-act function are related but not identical.

concepts.definition: A clause form conventionally associated with asking a question.
concepts.example: Is the train late? uses subject-auxiliary inversion.
concepts.false: Every interrogative begins with a wh-word.
concepts.note: Yes/no questions may use inversion without a wh-word; other languages use different resources.

concepts.definition: A clause form conventionally associated with directives.
concepts.example: Close the door uses a base-form verb and an understood addressee.
concepts.false: Every English imperative requires an overt subject before the verb.
concepts.note: Subjects are often unexpressed, though overt you and other special patterns are possible.

concepts.definition: A grammatical construction conventionally expressing an exclamatory evaluation.
concepts.example: What a lovely day it is! uses a characteristic exclamative pattern.
concepts.false: Every sentence with an exclamation mark must have exclamative syntax.
concepts.note: Punctuation and emotional delivery do not by themselves determine grammatical clause type.

concepts.definition: A sentence containing one independent clause and no subordinate clause.
concepts.example: Ali and Sara laughed and waved contains a single clause with coordinated elements.
concepts.false: A sentence becomes compound whenever it contains the word and.
concepts.note: Coordination of subjects or predicates does not necessarily introduce another independent clause.

concepts.definition: A sentence containing at least two coordinated independent clauses without subordinate clauses in the basic contrast.
concepts.example: Ali cooked, and Sara washed the dishes contains two independent clauses.
concepts.false: A compound sentence consists of one independent and one dependent clause only.
concepts.note: Coordination links units of equivalent syntactic status; subordinate clauses define a different structural relation.

concepts.definition: A sentence with one independent clause and at least one subordinate clause in the basic classification.
concepts.example: Although it rained, we played contains a subordinate clause and a main clause.
concepts.false: A complex sentence must have two independent clauses.
concepts.note: Complexity here concerns clause relations, not vocabulary difficulty or sheer length.

concepts.definition: A sentence with at least two independent clauses and at least one subordinate clause.
concepts.example: When it rained, Ali stayed home, but Sara went out combines both coordination and subordination.
concepts.false: A compound-complex sentence contains no subordinate clause.
concepts.note: Count clause status rather than merely counting verbs or conjunctions.

concepts.definition: Multiple interpretations associated with different grammatical groupings or attachments.
concepts.example: I saw the man with binoculars permits an instrument reading and a modifier-of-man reading.
concepts.false: Structural ambiguity always requires one word with two dictionary senses.
concepts.note: Lexical ambiguity involves word senses; structural ambiguity involves alternative structures.

concepts.definition: An alternative expression conveying substantially the same meaning in an intended context.
concepts.example: Sara gave Ali a book and Sara gave a book to Ali describe the same transfer in a suitable context.
concepts.false: Every paraphrase must use exactly the same words in the same order.
concepts.note: Differences in information structure or emphasis can remain despite close propositional equivalence.

concepts.definition: A construction in which an argument that is an object in a related active is promoted to subject in a typical English passive.
concepts.example: The door was opened by Ali corresponds to Ali opened the door.
concepts.false: The grammatical subject of a passive must be the semantic agent.
concepts.note: English verbal passives commonly use be plus a past participle; the agent phrase is often optional.

concepts.definition: An English construction placing an auxiliary before the subject in relevant clause types.
concepts.example: Can Sara swim? places can before Sara.
concepts.false: English yes/no questions always move the lexical main verb before the subject.
concepts.note: With no suitable auxiliary, English commonly uses do-support, as in Does Sara swim?

concepts.definition: A relationship between a wh-expression and the position interpreted as its argument or modifier site.
concepts.example: What did Sara buy? connects what with the understood object of buy.
concepts.false: What in What did Sara buy? has no relation to the thing bought.
concepts.note: Movement analyses model this as a dependency; theoretical accounts differ in implementation.

concepts.definition: Use of auxiliary do in certain English questions, negatives and emphatic constructions.
concepts.example: Did Ali leave? uses did with the base form leave.
concepts.false: Did Ali left? follows the ordinary standard English question pattern.
concepts.note: The auxiliary bears the finite tense marking, so the following lexical verb appears in its base form.

concepts.definition: Coordination or comparison using appropriately matched grammatical patterns.
concepts.example: She likes reading and swimming coordinates two similarly formed activities.
concepts.false: Parallel structure requires every coordinated expression to have a different grammatical form.
concepts.note: Parallelism supports clarity, though not every surface mismatch is automatically ungrammatical in all contexts.

concepts.definition: A rhetorical sentence arrangement presenting its main clause before added elaboration.
concepts.example: We reached Lahore that evening, tired after the long journey, presents its main assertion early.
concepts.false: A loose sentence must delay its main clause until its very end.
concepts.note: This is a rhetorical organization label, separate from simple/compound/complex clause classification.

concepts.definition: A rhetorical arrangement that delays completion of the main assertion until later.
concepts.example: After the storm had passed and the road reopened, we finally reached Lahore.
concepts.false: A periodic sentence is defined by having exactly two independent clauses.
concepts.note: Delayed completion creates anticipation; the label concerns rhetorical arrangement.

concepts.definition: Word order in which elements appear in an order differing from the relevant canonical pattern.
concepts.example: Here comes the bus places the verb before its subject.
concepts.false: Every fronted adverbial necessarily causes subject-verb inversion.
concepts.note: In Lahore, oranges grow fronts an adverbial but leaves the subject before its verb.

concepts.definition: A formal approach aiming to characterize the structures licensed by a linguistic system.
concepts.example: A finite set of structural rules is used to characterize an unbounded set of possible sentences.
concepts.false: Generative means a learner must memorize every possible complete sentence.
concepts.note: Generation is a formal notion about structural descriptions, not a claim that speakers consciously follow written rules.

concepts.definition: A family of generative models relating structures through transformations.
concepts.example: A historical model relates a question structure to an associated declarative configuration.
concepts.false: Transformational grammar claims that every transformation must preserve all meaning without exception.
concepts.note: Transformations and their interpretation vary across models; the lecture introduces a historical framework.

concepts.definition: An underlying syntactic representation in certain earlier transformational models.
concepts.example: A historical analysis distinguishes an underlying representation from an overtly realized structure.
concepts.false: Deep structure is a directly recorded acoustic waveform.
concepts.note: It is model-specific and is not a universal term for meaning in all modern syntactic theories.

concepts.definition: A syntactic representation resulting after transformations in certain historical models.
concepts.example: A historical account represents the output order of a passive separately from its underlying representation.
concepts.false: Surface structure simply means the ink on a printed page.
concepts.note: Even surface structure is an abstract syntactic representation rather than a raw sound signal or visual inscription.

concepts.definition: A diagnostic operation used as evidence that an expression forms a structural unit.
concepts.example: Replacing the old house with it tests the grouping in The old house collapsed.
concepts.false: A single failed movement test proves that an expression can never be a constituent.
concepts.note: Tests have constructional limits; converging evidence is stronger than relying on one diagnostic alone.

concepts.definition: The study of word and morpheme meanings and relations among lexical items.
concepts.example: An analyst compares the meanings of couch and sofa.
concepts.false: Lexical semantics is restricted to meanings of entire paragraphs and excludes words.
concepts.note: Phrasal or compositional semantics instead investigates how larger meanings are built.

concepts.definition: The study of how complex meanings arise from constituent meanings and their combination.
concepts.example: The analyst explains the difference between Dog bites man and Man bites dog.
concepts.false: Word order and grammatical structure never affect sentence meaning.
concepts.note: The same words can yield different meanings when their structural relations change.

concepts.definition: The entity or set of entities an expression applies to in a semantic interpretation.
concepts.example: In a suitable model, cat applies to the set of cats.
concepts.false: Denotation is simply any personal emotional association with a word.
concepts.note: Semantic denotations can be defined within models and need not be limited to objects currently visible.

concepts.definition: Associated social, emotional or evaluative meaning connected with an expression.
concepts.example: Home can evoke warmth or belonging beyond identifying a dwelling.
concepts.false: Connotation is guaranteed to be identical for every speaker in every situation.
concepts.note: Associations can vary across people, cultures and contexts, even when central descriptive meaning is shared.

concepts.definition: The set of entities satisfying an expression in a specified world or situation.
concepts.example: The extension of student at a university includes the individuals enrolled there at the relevant time.
concepts.false: An expression's extension can never change when the world changes.
concepts.note: Membership can vary across worlds and times while the descriptive concept remains relatively stable.

concepts.definition: The descriptive content or rule determining an expression's extension across relevant situations or worlds.
concepts.example: Planet applies according to a concept rather than merely listing currently named objects.
concepts.false: Intension is exactly the same as a person's private emotional reaction to a word.
concepts.note: Intension differs from connotation; in formal semantics it is often modelled as a function from worlds to extensions.

concepts.definition: The central descriptive content conventionally associated with an expression.
concepts.example: Needle is understood as a type of thin pointed implement in a relevant sense.
concepts.false: Conceptual meaning consists only of a listener's fear of injections.
concepts.note: Fear is an association; descriptive features identify the intended sense of the expression.

concepts.definition: A speaker's organized lexical knowledge, including forms, meanings and relevant grammatical properties.
concepts.example: A listener accesses a word's pronunciation and meaning during recognition.
concepts.false: The mental lexicon contains only a list of alphabetically printed pages.
concepts.note: It is a cognitive construct and need not be organized like a printed dictionary.

concepts.definition: A component or property used to represent a meaning contrast.
concepts.example: An analysis distinguishes adult from child using an adulthood feature.
concepts.false: Every lexical meaning can always be exhaustively represented by a tiny fixed feature list.
concepts.note: Feature analysis is useful for selected contrasts but faces difficult cases and theory-dependent choices.

concepts.definition: The range of senses or uses associated with a lexical item in a stated analysis.
concepts.example: Run appears in contexts about moving quickly, managing a shop and operating a machine.
concepts.false: A word's semantic range proves that every one of its senses fits every context.
concepts.note: Context and construction constrain which sense is intended.

concepts.definition: A semantic compatibility constraint or expectation on an expression's arguments.
concepts.example: The table drank tea is anomalous in an ordinary literal interpretation.
concepts.false: A selectional anomaly is automatically a word-order error.
concepts.note: Metaphor, personification and special contexts can support interpretations that violate ordinary literal expectations.

concepts.definition: A relation of identical or close meaning in the relevant sense and context.
concepts.example: Couch and sofa are near synonyms for a type of seating.
concepts.false: Near synonyms must be interchangeable in every idiom and social register.
concepts.note: Synonymy is often partial; collocation, register and nuance may differ.

concepts.definition: A broad relation of opposition in meaning.
concepts.example: Hot and cold contrast along a temperature dimension.
concepts.false: All antonyms necessarily form a binary opposition with no intermediate cases.
concepts.note: Gradable, complementary and relational oppositions should be distinguished.

concepts.definition: An opposition organized along a scale admitting intermediate values.
concepts.example: Something can be neither hot nor cold but warm.
concepts.false: Not hot must always entail cold.
concepts.note: Comparatives such as hotter and colder reflect the scalar nature of the contrast.

concepts.definition: A binary opposition in an idealized domain where one alternative excludes the other.
concepts.example: In an ordinary binary biological classification of an organism, alive contrasts with dead.
concepts.false: Every pair of complementary terms has a normal intermediate point on a degree scale.
concepts.note: The domain and interpretation matter; borderline biological or figurative cases require qualification.

concepts.definition: A relation in which opposed terms describe the same situation from different participant perspectives.
concepts.example: If A sold a book to B, B bought the book from A.
concepts.false: Buy and sell describe two unrelated events whenever a transfer occurs.
concepts.note: Converse relations reverse participant perspective rather than describing opposite temperatures on a scale.

concepts.definition: Distinct lexical items sharing a form with unrelated meanings.
concepts.example: Bank meaning a financial institution and bank meaning a river edge share a form.
concepts.false: Every pair of related senses of one word must be homonymy.
concepts.note: Distinguishing homonymy from polysemy can require historical and synchronic evidence.

concepts.definition: Identity of pronunciation between distinct lexical items.
concepts.example: Flour and flower sound alike in many English varieties.
concepts.false: Homophones must always have identical spelling.
concepts.note: Homophony concerns sound; spelling identity is a separate issue.

concepts.definition: Identity of spelling between lexical items or forms, whether or not pronunciation matches.
concepts.example: Lead meaning guide and lead meaning the metal share spelling but differ in pronunciation.
concepts.false: Homographs must always be pronounced identically.
concepts.note: Homography concerns the written form; some homographs are also homophones.

concepts.definition: Multiple related senses associated with one lexical item.
concepts.example: Head refers to a body part and also to the leader of an organization.
concepts.false: Polysemy requires unrelated words with coincidentally matching forms.
concepts.note: Relatedness of senses distinguishes the usual polysemy analysis from homonymy, though boundaries can be debated.

concepts.definition: A meaning relation in which one expression denotes a subtype of another.
concepts.example: Rose is a hyponym of flower.
concepts.false: Every flower must be a rose.
concepts.note: If an entity is a rose, it is a flower, but the reverse implication does not generally hold.

concepts.definition: A meaning relation in which one expression names a superordinate category.
concepts.example: Vehicle is a hypernym of bus.
concepts.false: Bus is more general than vehicle in the ordinary classification.
concepts.note: A hypernym includes the subtype in its extension; its descriptive content is usually less specific.

concepts.definition: A relation between subtypes sharing a superordinate category.
concepts.example: Bus and car are co-hyponyms under vehicle.
concepts.false: Co-hyponyms must always be synonyms.
concepts.note: Shared category membership does not make the subtypes identical in meaning.

concepts.definition: A part-whole lexical relation.
concepts.example: Wheel is a meronym of car in the relevant part-whole sense.
concepts.false: A wheel is a kind of car in the same way that a bus is a kind of vehicle.
concepts.note: Meronymy concerns parts; hyponymy concerns subtypes, so the relations are different.

concepts.definition: Reference through a salient association or contiguity between entities.
concepts.example: The White House announced a decision uses a building name for an institution or its officials.
concepts.false: Metonymy always depends on a comparison of similar shapes.
concepts.note: Association such as institution-for-people distinguishes it from resemblance-based metaphor.

concepts.definition: Interpretation of one domain or entity through another based on a perceived mapping or comparison.
concepts.example: Calling a fierce competitor a tiger attributes qualities without literally identifying a species.
concepts.false: Every metaphor is an ordinary literal claim that two entities are biologically identical.
concepts.note: Metaphorical interpretation draws on context and conceptual associations.

concepts.definition: A particularly representative exemplar of a category for a person or community.
concepts.example: A robin may be judged a more typical bird than a penguin in some communities.
concepts.false: A less typical bird is therefore not a member of the bird category.
concepts.note: Typicality is graded and culturally variable; category membership and typicality are distinct.

concepts.definition: Availability of more than one interpretation due to the lexical senses or identities of a form.
concepts.example: I waited at the bank leaves open a financial or river-side interpretation without further context.
concepts.false: Lexical ambiguity must always come from alternative phrase attachments.
concepts.note: Context can disambiguate lexical items, while attachment ambiguity concerns structure.

concepts.definition: A semantic role typically associated with an intentional initiator of an action.
concepts.example: Ali deliberately opened the door assigns Ali the agent role.
concepts.false: The agent must always be the grammatical subject, even in a passive.
concepts.note: In The door was opened by Ali, Ali remains agent while the door is subject.

concepts.definition: A semantic role for an entity undergoing movement, change or a relevant state in a given analysis.
concepts.example: The book moves in Sara carried the book upstairs.
concepts.false: Theme always means the intentional human initiator of an event.
concepts.note: Some frameworks distinguish patient from theme more narrowly; role inventories vary.

concepts.definition: A semantic role for a participant who perceives, feels or has a mental state.
concepts.example: Sara is the experiencer in Sara fears spiders.
concepts.false: An experiencer must intentionally cause the emotion experienced.
concepts.note: Experiencers need not control their state and are distinct from intentional agents.

concepts.definition: A semantic role for the means used to carry out an action.
concepts.example: A key is the instrument in Ali opened the door with a key.
concepts.false: Instrument refers to the destination of a movement event.
concepts.note: A participant used as a means differs from an agent initiating the action.

concepts.definition: A semantic role identifying where a state or event occurs.
concepts.example: In Lahore supplies location in Sara worked in Lahore.
concepts.false: Location necessarily describes the point of origin of every movement.
concepts.note: Source and goal concern origin and destination, while location concerns where something is situated.

concepts.definition: Semantic roles identifying a movement's origin and destination respectively.
concepts.example: From Lahore is source and to Karachi is goal in The parcel travelled from Lahore to Karachi.
concepts.false: Source and goal always identify the same endpoint by definition.
concepts.note: The roles distinguish direction even when neither expression is the grammatical subject.

concepts.definition: Semantic roles identifying ownership and nonintentional causal contribution, respectively.
concepts.example: Ali has a bicycle assigns a possessor; The wind broke the branch assigns a natural cause.
concepts.false: A natural force must be an intentional human agent whenever it causes a change.
concepts.note: Cause is often called causer; some inventories include natural forces under a broader agent label.

concepts.definition: A relation where the truth of one proposition guarantees another's truth under the intended interpretation.
concepts.example: Sara owns a red car entails that Sara owns a car.
concepts.false: An entailment may be cancelled while keeping the original proposition true in the same interpretation.
concepts.note: Entailment is a truth-based relation, unlike a defeasible conversational suggestion.

concepts.definition: Incompatibility between propositions that cannot both be true in the same relevant interpretation.
concepts.example: Ali is asleep and Ali is not asleep conflict when time and intended sense are held fixed.
concepts.false: Any two sentences with different words must contradict one another.
concepts.note: Hold reference, time and meaning constant before diagnosing a contradiction.

concepts.definition: A proposition true by its logical form in the intended classical analysis.
concepts.example: It is raining or it is not raining exemplifies excluded middle in classical logic.
concepts.false: A tautology is defined as an empirical weather prediction that may turn out false.
concepts.note: Logical truth differs from ordinary factual truth; pragmatic use can still make a tautology informative in context.

concepts.definition: The message or intention a speaker communicates in a particular use.
concepts.example: A teacher says It is noisy here to encourage the class to quieten down.
concepts.false: Speaker meaning must always equal the dictionary meaning of each isolated word.
concepts.note: Interpreting an intention uses the utterance plus evidence about context; it is not unrestricted mind-reading.

concepts.definition: The surrounding language that supports interpretation of an expression.
concepts.example: In Sara bought a book. She read it, preceding expressions help interpret she and it.
concepts.false: Linguistic context consists only of the physical room where people are standing.
concepts.note: Also called co-text, it differs from physical and wider social circumstances.

concepts.definition: Relevant features of the communicative situation and shared background.
concepts.example: A warning about a coming car is interpreted differently beside a road than in a delivery discussion.
concepts.false: Situational context excludes who the speaker and hearer are.
concepts.note: Participants, place, time, purposes and assumed background can all affect interpretation.

concepts.definition: Information participants treat as shared for the purposes of their interaction.
concepts.example: Two colleagues refer to the meeting because both know which scheduled meeting is relevant.
concepts.false: Common ground must consist of facts known by every human being.
concepts.note: Shared assumptions can be local to an interaction and can be mistaken or negotiated.

concepts.definition: A defeasible meaning inferred from an utterance and conversational reasoning beyond what is explicitly said.
concepts.example: Some students passed may suggest not all, though the speaker can add in fact all did.
concepts.false: Every conversational implicature is a noncancellable logical entailment.
concepts.note: Implicatures depend on contextual assumptions and can often be cancelled without contradiction.

concepts.definition: Grice's framework for reasoning about contributions appropriate to an accepted conversational purpose.
concepts.example: A listener interprets an apparently indirect reply as relevant to the ongoing discussion.
concepts.false: The cooperative principle guarantees that speakers are friendly and tell the truth.
concepts.note: It is an interpretive framework, not a claim that every actual conversation is morally cooperative.

concepts.definition: A conversational expectation to provide the amount of information required for the exchange.
concepts.example: Asked for an exact appointment time, a speaker supplies ten thirty rather than only sometime.
concepts.false: Quantity requires speakers to give every fact they know on every occasion.
concepts.note: Appropriate informativeness depends on the purpose of the exchange, not maximum verbosity.

concepts.definition: A conversational expectation to avoid falsehood and claims without adequate evidence.
concepts.example: A researcher qualifies an uncertain result rather than presenting a guess as established fact.
concepts.false: Quality requires making confident claims even when there is no evidence.
concepts.note: Sincerity and evidential support distinguish quality from manner and quantity.

concepts.definition: A conversational expectation that contributions be relevant to the exchange.
concepts.example: Asked where to buy fuel, a speaker mentions a nearby open petrol station.
concepts.false: The relation maxim concerns only whether an utterance is pronounced loudly.
concepts.note: Relevance may be indirect; the listener can infer how a response bears on the current purpose.

concepts.definition: A conversational expectation favoring clarity, order and avoidance of obscurity or unnecessary ambiguity.
concepts.example: A speaker gives ordered directions in clear language.
concepts.false: Manner is the maxim specifically requiring adequate evidence for factual claims.
concepts.note: Manner concerns how something is expressed; evidential truthfulness belongs to quality.

concepts.definition: An overt apparent failure to satisfy a maxim that invites an additional interpretation.
concepts.example: During heavy rain, a speaker says Lovely weather! with an obviously ironic delivery.
concepts.false: Flouting is defined as secretly deceiving the listener without any recoverable signal.
concepts.note: A conspicuous mismatch can prompt implicature; flouting differs from covert violation.

concepts.definition: A covert failure to satisfy a conversational maxim, potentially misleading the listener.
concepts.example: Someone knowingly gives a false alibi while intending it to be believed.
concepts.false: Every violation is a transparent invitation to infer irony.
concepts.note: Whether a maxim is flouted or violated depends on the interaction and the speaker's apparent communicative stance.

concepts.definition: Producing an utterance with a linguistic form and propositional meaning in speech-act analysis.
concepts.example: A speaker utters The gate is open with its ordinary sentence meaning.
concepts.false: Locutionary act means only the psychological effect on a frightened listener.
concepts.note: Locution concerns saying something; illocution concerns the act performed in saying it.

concepts.definition: The communicative act performed in saying something, such as warning, requesting or promising.
concepts.example: Saying The gate is open functions as a warning that a child may leave.
concepts.false: Illocutionary force is identical to the physical volume of the voice.
concepts.note: The same sentence can perform different acts in different contexts.

concepts.definition: An effect of an utterance on a hearer's actions, feelings or beliefs.
concepts.example: A warning causes a listener to move away from a road.
concepts.false: A warning has no illocutionary force unless the listener actually becomes afraid.
concepts.note: Intended communicative act and actual consequence differ; an appropriate warning may fail to persuade.

concepts.definition: An act whose typical communicative function aligns with the conventional function of its clause form.
concepts.example: Close the door is used straightforwardly to command closure.
concepts.false: A direct speech act must contain a performative verb such as promise.
concepts.note: Directness concerns the relation between form and function, not merely whether a verb is explicitly named.

concepts.definition: An act communicated through a form conventionally associated with another function.
concepts.example: Could you pass the salt? is used as a request rather than a test of physical ability.
concepts.false: Every interrogative utterance can function only as a request for information.
concepts.note: Listeners infer the intended act from conventions, context and background assumptions.

concepts.definition: An utterance that explicitly names the act it performs in appropriate circumstances.
concepts.example: I promise to return the book tomorrow names the commitment being made.
concepts.false: The past report I promised yesterday necessarily makes a new promise now.
concepts.note: First-person present use is a common pattern, but felicity and actual communicative use also matter.

concepts.definition: Conditions required for a speech act to be appropriate or successful in a relevant sense.
concepts.example: An institutional declaration succeeds only when authority and procedures are appropriate.
concepts.false: Any institutional formula works equally well when spoken by an unauthorized passer-by.
concepts.note: Conditions differ across acts and may concern authority, circumstances, sincerity and commitment.

concepts.definition: A speech-act class committing the speaker to the truth of a proposition.
concepts.example: A witness states that the door was locked.
concepts.false: An assertive is defined solely as an attempt to get someone else to act.
concepts.note: Assertions and reports concern truth commitment, while directives seek action from a hearer.
