concepts.definition: A speech-act class aiming to get an addressee to do something.
concepts.example: A teacher asks the class to open their books.
concepts.false: A directive necessarily commits the speaker to a future action of their own.
concepts.note: Requests and commands are directives; speaker commitments characterize commissives.

concepts.definition: A speech-act class committing the speaker to a future course of action.
concepts.example: A student promises to submit the assignment tomorrow.
concepts.false: Commissives only describe the present temperature.
concepts.note: Promises and some offers commit a speaker, subject to the context and the act's conditions.

concepts.definition: A speech-act class expressing an attitude or psychological state about a situation.
concepts.example: A speaker apologizes for arriving late.
concepts.false: Every expressive changes a person's legal status through institutional authority.
concepts.note: Apologies and congratulations express attitudes; declarations require a different institutional relation.

concepts.definition: A speech act that changes an institutional state when successfully performed by an appropriate person.
concepts.example: An authorized judge pronounces a sentence in court.
concepts.false: Anyone can successfully declare a defendant legally guilty in any casual conversation.
concepts.note: Institutional authority and procedures distinguish declarations from ordinary assertions about a legal outcome.

concepts.definition: Background information presented as already taken for granted in an utterance.
concepts.example: Sara stopped smoking normally presupposes that she used to smoke.
concepts.false: A presupposition must always be true in the actual world.
concepts.note: Speakers can presuppose something false; hearers may challenge or accommodate it.

concepts.definition: The tendency of some presuppositions to survive under negation or other operators.
concepts.example: Sara did not stop smoking commonly still suggests that Sara smoked before.
concepts.false: Negating an utterance always removes every presupposition associated with it.
concepts.note: Projection is context-sensitive and differs across triggers; survival under negation is a useful diagnostic, not an exceptionless rule.

concepts.definition: An expression conventionally associated with presupposing the truth of its complement.
concepts.example: Sara regrets that she missed the bus normally takes the missed bus as background fact.
concepts.false: Regret normally presupposes that its complement is false.
concepts.note: Compare believe: believing a proposition does not by itself make it factive.

concepts.definition: Context-dependent reference anchored to participants in the speech event.
concepts.example: I refers to the current speaker in an ordinary unquoted utterance.
concepts.false: I always refers to the same named individual regardless of who is speaking.
concepts.note: The conventional meaning identifies a participant role; context supplies the particular referent.

concepts.definition: Context-dependent reference to locations relative to a deictic anchor.
concepts.example: Put it here depends on the speaker's or another established spatial viewpoint.
concepts.false: Here has one unchanging geographical referent in every utterance.
concepts.note: The deictic centre can shift in narrative or reported discourse.

concepts.definition: Context-dependent reference to time relative to an utterance or other established anchor.
concepts.example: Tomorrow normally denotes the day after the day of speaking.
concepts.false: Tomorrow names the same calendar date in every conversation.
concepts.note: The anchor matters; quotation and narrative can change the relevant reference time.

concepts.definition: Linguistic marking that indexes social relationships or status.
concepts.example: Choosing a respectful address form signals the relationship between participants.
concepts.false: Social deixis is defined as the acoustic frequency of a vowel.
concepts.note: Honorifics and address choices can index status without literally describing physical distance.

concepts.definition: Reference to a portion of discourse as discourse.
concepts.example: That was a strange thing to say uses that to point to a preceding utterance.
concepts.false: Discourse deixis must always refer to an object physically beside the speaker.
concepts.note: It differs from ordinary object reference, though the boundary with anaphora can require careful analysis.

concepts.definition: Interpretation of an expression through an antecedent in discourse.
concepts.example: Sara found a key and put it in her bag uses it for the previously mentioned key.
concepts.false: Every pronoun must point to something physically present and can never have a textual antecedent.
concepts.note: Pronouns may be anaphoric or deictic, so pronoun form alone does not establish the reference mechanism.

concepts.definition: Updating the shared assumptions to make an utterance's presupposition interpretable when appropriate.
concepts.example: Hearing My sister is visiting, a listener provisionally accepts that the speaker has a sister.
concepts.false: Accommodation requires the hearer to accept every presupposition as unquestionably true.
concepts.note: A hearer may instead challenge an assumption; accommodation is a contextual interpretive move.

concepts.definition: A characterization emphasizing human symbolic communication of ideas, emotions and desires.
concepts.example: A definition groups communicating ideas with expressing feelings and wishes through symbols.
concepts.false: Sapir's definition in the handout defines language solely as a set of mathematical sentences.
concepts.note: This is a paraphrase of the handout's historical definition, not an endorsement that natural signed languages should be excluded.

concepts.definition: A characterization emphasizing arbitrary vocal symbols enabling social cooperation.
concepts.example: A definition relates a group's cooperation to a conventional system of speech symbols.
concepts.false: Bloch and Trager's definition in the handout excludes any role for a social group.
concepts.note: Its vocal emphasis reflects a historical formulation; contemporary accounts include signed languages.

concepts.definition: A characterization emphasizing language as an institution for human communication and interaction using habitual symbols.
concepts.example: A definition highlights an institution through which humans interact by established oral-auditory symbols.
concepts.false: Hall's historical definition in the handout concerns only spelling and printing.
concepts.note: The historical oral-auditory emphasis should be distinguished from the broader modern recognition of signed language.

concepts.definition: A characterization of a language as a set of sentences constructed from a finite inventory of elements.
concepts.example: A finite vocabulary and structural resources support potentially unbounded sentence formation.
concepts.false: A potentially infinite language requires each individual sentence to contain infinitely many words.
concepts.note: An unbounded set can consist of individual sentences that are each finite in length.

concepts.definition: A motivated resemblance between aspects of a linguistic form and its meaning.
concepts.example: An onomatopoeic word imitates an associated sound to some degree.
concepts.false: The presence of iconic forms proves that no other linguistic signs can be arbitrary.
concepts.note: Iconicity and convention can coexist; sound-symbolic forms differ across languages.

concepts.definition: A broad teaching label for investigation of language in relation to wider social, psychological or other domains.
concepts.example: A course groups sociolinguistics and psycholinguistics as analyses beyond internal structure alone.
concepts.false: Macrolinguistics means that core language structures are irrelevant to all interdisciplinary work.
concepts.note: Micro/macro terminology is useful for orientation but its boundaries vary across textbooks.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: Deliberate efforts to influence a community's language practices, status or resources.
concepts.example: A policy develops terminology and literacy materials for a regional language.
concepts.false: Language planning concerns only an individual's tongue position during one consonant.
concepts.note: Status planning and corpus planning address different but connected dimensions of language policy.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: Variation in language associated with a communicative situation, purpose or activity.
concepts.example: The same speaker uses different wording in a research article and a family message.
concepts.false: Register is determined solely by a speaker's birthplace and cannot change with context.
concepts.note: Register differs from regional dialect, although both can shape a text.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 1–10: areas and methods; field definitions in supplied lecture

concepts.definition: Articulation just behind the alveolar ridge.
concepts.example: English [ʃ] in ship is commonly described as postalveolar.
concepts.false: English [ʃ] must be produced with both lips fully closed.
concepts.note: Some introductory books use broader palatal labels; more precise IPA descriptions separate postalveolar and palatal places.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Articulation involving the tongue body and the hard palate.
concepts.example: [j] in yes is a palatal approximant.
concepts.false: A palatal consonant is defined by contact between the lower lip and upper teeth.
concepts.note: Palatal [j] differs in place from the velar consonant [k].
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: An approximant whose airflow passes around one or both sides of the tongue.
concepts.example: English [l] allows lateral oral airflow.
concepts.false: A lateral approximant requires all airflow to pass only through the nose.
concepts.note: Lateral refers to airflow; English /l/ can have different context-dependent realizations.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A period of voiceless airflow associated with the release of a stop, marked [ʰ] in IPA.
concepts.example: The [pʰ] in a typical stressed English pin has an audible puff of air.
concepts.false: Aspiration is identical to the voiced vibration of [z].
concepts.note: In English it is often predictable for voiceless stops; its contrastive status differs across languages.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Organization of segments into units commonly analyzed as onset, nucleus and coda.
concepts.example: Cat has /k/ as onset, /æ/ as nucleus and /t/ as coda in a simple analysis.
concepts.false: Every syllable in every language must contain an overt consonant onset.
concepts.note: The nucleus is the sonority peak; some languages permit syllabic consonants.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: Related physical measures associated with signal magnitude and energy.
concepts.example: A sound recording displays greater waveform excursions when amplitude increases.
concepts.false: Greater amplitude by definition means that a word has more morphemes.
concepts.note: Loudness is a perceptual correlate, not simply another name for a physical amplitude measurement.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: The time interval occupied by an event or speech segment.
concepts.example: A vowel lasts 150 milliseconds in a recorded token.
concepts.false: Duration is measured in hertz rather than units of time.
concepts.note: Physical duration can affect contrasts, stress and rhythm, depending on the language.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 2–4: speech sounds, transcription and contrast

concepts.definition: A hierarchy of grammatical units in a stated framework.
concepts.example: Sentence, clause, phrase, word and morpheme are arranged from larger to smaller units in an introductory scale.
concepts.false: Syntax itself is a grammatical unit on the same rank scale as word.
concepts.note: Syntax names a field or level of analysis, not a unit equivalent to sentence on this scale.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A word class that readily admits new members.
concepts.example: English gains new nouns and verbs for new technologies.
concepts.false: An open lexical class is defined by being unable to gain new words.
concepts.note: Openness is a tendency; nouns, verbs and adjectives are common examples.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: A word class with relatively limited membership and limited ready addition.
concepts.example: English personal pronouns form a comparatively restricted inventory.
concepts.false: A closed class can never change in any way over historical time.
concepts.note: Closed means comparatively resistant to expansion, not eternally frozen.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: The conventional introductory list of eight English inflectional suffix categories.
concepts.example: Plural, possessive, third-person singular, past tense, two participles, comparative and superlative are listed.
concepts.false: Agentive -er in teacher belongs to the eight ordinary English inflectional suffix categories.
concepts.note: Comparative -er in taller is inflectional; the similar-looking agentive -er is derivational.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Forming a word by combining portions of existing words.
concepts.example: Brunch combines parts of breakfast and lunch.
concepts.false: Blending requires retaining both complete words in every case.
concepts.note: It differs from ordinary compounding in which whole lexical bases are combined.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Forming a shorter lexical form by shortening an existing word.
concepts.example: Exam is a shortened form of examination.
concepts.false: Clipping requires adding a new derivational suffix.
concepts.note: Shortening does not necessarily change the word's core referential meaning or category.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Forming a word from initial letters that is pronounced as a word in a narrow usage.
concepts.example: NASA is pronounced as a word rather than as a sequence of individual letter names.
concepts.false: Every initial-letter abbreviation must be pronounced as one word.
concepts.note: Terminology varies; the narrow contrast distinguishes acronyms from initialisms such as BBC.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: Adoption of a linguistic form from another language.
concepts.example: English uses bungalow, historically borrowed from an Indian-language source.
concepts.false: A borrowed word must permanently retain every phonetic property of its source language.
concepts.note: Borrowings often become adapted to the receiving language's sounds and morphology.
concepts.referenceSection: Chs. 6–8: word forms, word classes and phrases

concepts.definition: An explicit framework aiming to describe or explain linguistic patterns.
concepts.example: A grammar proposes structural representations and tests whether they account for speaker judgments.
concepts.false: A linguistic theory is simply any unsupported personal preference about elegant writing.
concepts.note: Theoretical assumptions should be distinguished from observations and evaluated against evidence.

concepts.definition: Patterns of pronunciation associated with an individual or variety.
concepts.example: Two speakers use similar grammar but pronounce the same vowels differently.
concepts.false: Accent necessarily includes every difference in vocabulary and clause structure.
concepts.note: Dialect is a broader label; everyone has an accent in the descriptive sense.

concepts.definition: Investigation emphasizing how language relates to the organization and functioning of society.
concepts.example: A study examines institutional language distribution in education and administration.
concepts.false: Sociology of language is defined only by measuring the acoustic spectrum of vowels.
concepts.note: It overlaps sociolinguistics, but often foregrounds societal institutions and language functions.

concepts.definition: An expression's linguistic meaning and its relations within a language, distinguished from particular reference.
concepts.example: Morning star and evening star differ in sense even when both refer to Venus.
concepts.false: Two expressions with the same referent must have identical sense.
concepts.note: Co-reference does not require identical descriptive or cognitive content.

concepts.definition: The use of an expression to identify an entity in context.
concepts.example: A speaker uses that student to identify a particular person in the room.
concepts.false: Reference is identical to every emotional association a hearer has with a word.
concepts.note: Referential interpretation draws on linguistic meaning and contextual information.

concepts.definition: A statement true in virtue of meanings under an adopted semantic analysis.
concepts.example: Every bachelor is unmarried is an introductory example using the ordinary adult-person sense.
concepts.false: An analytic statement is defined as one requiring a survey to discover whether its words mean what they do.
concepts.note: Examples depend on the stipulated sense; social and institutional uses can complicate apparently simple definitions.
